title: S+ Review Guide
points: History S+ Review Guide Writer: Alice Wang 10 (12) Editor: Leon Gooi 10 (12) Range: Causes of WWII-Cold War Note: Review Guide are UNOFFICIAL sources of reference and do NOT include or hint at questions in the actual exam!

G10 PA Resource Department Semester 2 Finals Review Guide Causes of WW2 (1939 -1945 ) 1) Unresolved problems from the Treaty of Versailles-Germany and its allies were held responsible for all destruction and costs from the Treaty of Versailles where they lost territory, were forced to pay huge reparations, take responsibility for WW1 through the war guilt clause, and forced to demilitarize their nation-this resulted in Germany suffering from inflation and unemployment due to their inability to pay the reparati ons-Germany felt bitter and desperate, they wanted freedom and territory back-resulted in a strong ambition for Germany to make a comeback in WW2 2) Great Depression and (which led to) the Rise of Dictatorships-The American Wall Street Crash of October 1929 made the world suffer from ‘Great Depression ’ where a chain reaction occurred: Due to America ’s need to pay for their own debts, Germany couldn ’t seek financial support to pay their reparations anymore, and France and Britain hence wouldn ’t make their loa n payments to Germany anymore-While the current governments were unable to revive their countries, totalitarian leaders arose-Totalitarianism refers to a system of government in which one party tries to rule with complete control over every aspect of the l ives of its citizen-Totalitarian leaders: Joseph Stalin of USSR (communist), Adolf Hitler of Germany (fascism), Benito Mussolini of Italy (fascism), Emperor Hirohito of Japan (constitutional monarch) - Though these leaders had different ideologies, they all thrive towards MILITARISM + NATIONALISM which are key factors that led them to aggressively demand control over other nations 3) Failure of the League of Nations-The League of Nations was an international forum and an international collective security arrangement where nations that joined agreed to settle disputes rather than engage in war Why it’s considered ‘failure ’: - Since the US, as a major power, refused to join the League of Nations, countries grew suspicious-1931, when Japan invaded Manchuria (no rtheastern of china), the League did not stop the Japanese-1935, Italy invaded Abyssinia (current day Ethiopia) but instead of helping, Britain and France signed a secret pact to give Abyssinia to Italy-Meanwhile these invasions, Germany also left the League and rearmed itself; league called for a disarmament conference but Germany ignored it, it instead stated to regain territories like Rhineland-Conclusion: the League of Nations resulted in severe distrust between nations; small nations were neglected and lots of countries disobeyed its rules 4) Appeasement (1935 -1939) - Britain and France determined that engaging in conflict with Germany will result in a devastating war like WWI done mainly by British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain-Main reasons: Britain wasn ’t prepared for war, some felt sympathetic for Hitler and his complaints-appeasements included granting Hitler land, control over nations, and the freedom to remilitarize-greatest example for appeasement: Munich Agreement-Stakes of appeasement: Britain and France willin gly gave Germany Sudetenland (western Czechoslovakia which had German -speaking people) as long as Hitler promised to not g further-German citizens found this reasonable because Hitler claimed that he wanted to unite all German speaking people into the Third Reich (Nazi Germany) - Anschluss was also created, dedicated to Germany ’s future expansion; it ’s a union between Austria and Germany in 1938 beca use Austria provided strategic land, resources, and soldiers that were adequate for Germany exploitation-Though Chamberlain felt confidence that British will finally be in peace, Winston Churchill (a British statesmen) stron gly opposed appeasement since he knew that Hitler ’s footsteps would not stop there after annexing Sudetenland-Conclusion: appeasement resulted in WW2 because Hitler developed unstoppable hubris, he became even more demanding-imperialism 5) The invasion of Poland-OFFICIAL/DIRECT CAUSE FOR WW2 by Hitle r-Britain, France, Russia previously formed an alliance called the Allied powers-August 1939, Russia left that alliance and instead joined Hitler; signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact - a nona ggression pact that publicly stated that the rival nations would maintain peaceful relations-they agreed to divide Poland into ‘spheres of influence ’ where Germany gets western Poland, USSR gets eastern Poland-September 1st

1939, Germany invades Poland with the power of blitzkrieg (lighting war-defeating opponents using a series of short military campaigns ) which caused lots of immediate harm to Poland (how they won) - German ’s Luftwaffe was a critical part of blitzkrieg-September 17th 1939, USSR occupied Eastern Poland-Poland ’s location was geographically vulnerable due to it ’s location right between USSR and Germany-Context about Hitler ’s invasion on Poland: he claimed that ethnic Germans living in Poland needed protection (excuse to invade Poland),

Britain and France declared war on Hitler (they realized appeasement failed), Hitler had panzers (tanks) and well-trained army (secretly in the past years, violating the treaty of versailles) 6) Other Causes (also causes of WW1) - M.A.I.N-Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism-Alliances: 1) Axis Powers: Germany, Italy, Japan 2) Allies Powers: U.S., Britain, France-USSR-originally allied with Axis powers until Germany invaded USSR in 1941 The 2 Theaters of WW2-Pacific and European-65 million estimated total worldwide deaths;

40 million are civilians 1) European Theater (significant statistics) - 150 trillion ways for German ‘enigma ’ machine to encode a single letter-400,000 tons of supplies delivered to the Allied Front in France - 9.5 million estimated peak strength of the German armed forced during WW2-7600 women ’s army corps members serving in European theater by 1945-portrays women ’s increasing authority 2) Pacific Theater (significant statistics) - 3 atomic bombs denoted by the US during WW2-115,000 square miles of ocean covered in battles-20 million estimated deaths in China as a result of WW2-china contributed to ww2 by resisting Japanese aggression, on the allies powers side General Comparison: 1) Geography: - European theater had dense continent, land -based-Pacific theater had vast oceans, island chains, naval/marine -based, US-led 2) Technology in Military (based on 1) - European theater: tanks, artillery, machine guns, code breaking (enigma from Germany), V2 rockets-Pacific theater: aircraft carriers, nuclear bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, submarines, planes 3) Deaths: - European theater: 15-20 million military deaths, 30 -35 million civilian deaths (more deadly) - Pacific theater: 4 million military deaths, 10-12 million civilian deaths U.S.

Entry in WW2 Context-Due to the 1)Great Depression which brought severe economic damage and political instability to the US as well as 2)the trauma from WW1; the US developed a mood of isolationism where the country want to intervene in anymore bloody conflicts-Woodrow Wilson (previous president who wanted to join League of Nations but was blocked by congress) was replaced by Warren G.

Harding who refuses (which aligns with what the citizens wanted) to join war, claiming the US needs to ‘return to normalcy ’ US still sinked in Isolationism-Neutralit y Acts: passed by US Congress which banned American citizens from trading with nations at war, loaning them money, or traveling on their ships-this was passed down after the failure of the League of Nations-US believed that still no nation posed any direct threats US getting indirectly involved-1932, President FDR (Franklin Delano Roosevelt) insisted on participating in WW2, but due to limitations set by neutrality acts, he decided to indirectly get involved in WW2 first-1939 November; American manufacturers were allowed to sell arms and supplies to nations at war-allowed British to buy American goods as long as paid up front and transported them in their own ships-1941 March; after Hitler conquered France and Britain wa s the ’one man standing ’, US passed the Lend -Lease Act which authorized US to lend war supplies to nations whose defense he deemed ‘vital to the defense of the US ’; he said the best policy to keep US out of war was to become the ‘Arsenal of Democracy ’ - 1941 August; Roosevelt and Churchill met on the Atlantic charter that talked about their desire to preserve peace and their commitment to working together later on for the war US getting directly involved-1941 December 7th; Japanese carrier planes att acked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii which knocked out the pride of the US pacific fleet; one day later Congress declared war on Japan, Italy, and Germany declared war on the US-US strategy: ‘Germany first’ strate gy (brought up by Churchill and Roosevelt) where they believed though the Japanese attacked, Germany was more threatening War on the Eastern Front (Battle of Stalin grad/ Operation Barbarossa ) Context-More combatants were killed on the Eastern Front than in all other theaters of WW2 combined-1923, Hitler wrote Mein Kampf /“My Struggle ” which said: - Territorial expansion, racially pure state, desturction of Jews (laid ideological groundwork for the Holocaust) - he believed in Germany ’s destiny to defeat a historic enemy-France, and pushing eastward into the USSR to exterminate communists and Slavs but he knew fighting both at once wasn ’t feasible (led to next bullet point) - 1939 August, Hitler signed Nazi -Soviet Pact-divide Poland, Baltic States (Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia), Rom ania, Finland into German and Soviet spheres of influence; Germany gets west Poland, USSR gets east (strategically befriending USSR) - Hitler ’s Purpose: avoid conflict with USSR when seizing Poland and France; he said “the sooner Russia is smashed the better ” - Hitler ’s wanted gains from winning this battle: exterminate slavs, exterminate communism, gain access to valuable resources-1939 September; Germany and USSR both invade Poland The War-1941 June 22; Operation Barbarossa: 3 million man invasion by Hitler of USSR (hitler was hubristic, he believed USSR would be easy to defeat because its g enerals were inept and some political instabilit y democratically since some opposed Stalin ’s regime )

Successful in early stages but later the Red Army (led by Bolsheviks/communists) made a major comeback (Red army was the largest in the world with vast natural resources) and won-US and UK united with USSR since they had a common enemy-Nazi Germany; so they together fought in the battle of Stalingrad-Atrocities including beheadings and mass rapes occurred on a daily basis-millions of captured soldiers died of exposure and maltreatment-inhumane conditions-Hitler lost majorly due to overwhelming determination-refused to retreat despite substantial casualties-Late 1942: German General Blumentritt after visiting eastern front said: “there was little timber available for constructing defenses, there were no proper trenches or fixed positions ” so he suggested a step back but Hitler neglected it-1942 -1943: soldiers say “I would eat a cat ”, “this isn ’t hell, this is ten times worse than hell ” - due to an arctic winter, Germans stopped with imperialism before Moscow-1942 July 28: STRONG NATIONALISM AND DEDICATION on both sides: Hitler wanted to wipe ut males and deport females; Russian General Chuikov says “we will defend the city or die ” - Deaths: Axis powers: 850,000; Soviets: 750,000-Significance of the Battle of Stalingrad: marked Hitler ’s first major defeat and a shift in alliance where the USSR joins the allies powers Wars in the European Theater (1941 -1945 ) 1）Mid 1942: Allies agreed on a ‘German First ’ Strate gy-allies all reached consensus on the fact that Japan was much of a smaller threat compared to
Germany 2）November 1942: Operation Torch-The invasion of North Africa-Why?

Original plan was for Generals George Marshall and Dwight Eisenhower to invade German occupied France directly in order to distract German troops from fighting the USSR by opening up a second front; but this wasn ’t feasible due to the lack of mobilization of the US army-This was Eisenhower ’s first combat assignment-Allies landed in Morocco and Algeria, then moved toward Tunisia (east) but they suffered some setbacks at Kasserine Pass (Feb 1943) but in 2 m onths they trapped numerous axis troops-they won

3）January 1943 (near the end of Operation Torch): Casablanca Conference (held in Casablanca which is northwest of Morocco ) - where Roosevelt and Churchill met to decide future military plans-outcomes: pursue the unconditional surrender of the axis powers, plan to invade Sicily first, then get to mainland Italy 4）July-September 1943: Invasion of Sicily (Operation Husky) and Italy-under Generals George Patton and Montgomery-Sicily immediately surrendered but Hitler ordered to fight to the last man to keep Italy-Later, the allies bombed Berlin (Nazi

Production centers, nearly annihilating the Luftwaffe-the German Air Force, crucial for the success of D -DAY) Belgium and Northern France-In the bombing of Berlin, the allies knew they were gonna face the most powerful air defense system in the world-Dogfighting: a close combat between military aircraft 5）June 4 1944: Invasion of Italy-Kesselring (German military leader ) led this fight for Germany; driving the allied invasion force back into the sea at Salerno (southeast of Italy, aka.

Toe of Italy) - his key military strategy: he engined the Gustav line: brilliant defensive entanglement of machine guns, booby traps, and min es stitched into Italy ’s mountains-June 4, allies conquer Rome 6）June 6 1944: D-DAY!!!

Invasion of Normandy (Operation Overlord ) - largest amphibious (land and water) war in WW2-reason for success: allies invaded surprisingly-invaded Normandy instead of Calais where the channel was far narrower and axis defenses were stronger-Under Eisenhower, allied forces liberated Paris and Northern France and Belgium-Liberation of Paris: - august 25 1944, germany surrendered Paris to allies-opened up war on the western front-making Germany fight in both eastern and western front-Allied advancements slowed down after liberating Paris because there were disagreements among them where they wanted to undergo different strategies (between indirect and direct; slowed down decision making and delayed offensives) Specifics of the War: - Harsh conditions of this attack: the English Channel had rough seas and unpredictable weather and formidable beach obstacles-pre-war; people said “we were getting ready for one of the biggest adventures of our lives ” - Midnight June 6, allies started attacking, they first sabotaged bridges and railroad lines to prevent defense from axis powers-they then landed the largest amphibious force moving through the storm -tossed waters toward the beaches-Americans were packed into flat -bottomed Higgins boats with vomit filling the bottom of the boats-Landing - 5 beaches: British and Canadians landed at Juno, Gold, Sword beaches; Americans landed at Omaha and Utah beaches-Omaha beach had the fierces t fighting due to steep cliffs; but Americans annihilated Omaha beach at a heavy cost with a loss rate over 13% - Artillery Battalion says “if you thought about the possibilities of what lay ahead, it was more than your mind could take” - Military Strategy: Red Ball Express-an American truck convoy (g roups ) system which operated 24/7 with many African American drivers whom supplied sufficient fuel, ammunition, and other vital supplies to the American and allied forces advancing through France and Belgium after landing on Normand y-why the name?

The system utilized designated routes marked with red balls and the trucks had labels of red balls for identification; so people could free up roads for coming troops-Significance: if D -Day had f ailed, attacks would not have been possible for another year, which would have given Hitler time to strengthen the Atlantic Wall, harass England with the newly developed v1 flying bombs and v2 rockets 2) September 1944: Operation Market Garden-Failure-flawed plan to capture key bridges in the Netherlands and enter Germany quickly

Allies attempted to break into the heart of Germany but fought losses with small gains - ‘the wrong time, the wrong place ” - Germany had it all equipped-allied losses: 12,00; over 250 aircrafts shot down 3) December 16 1944: Battle of the Bulge-largest American infantry (land soldiers) war-Hitler launched panzer units through the Ardennes Forest and pushed the allies far back that created a ‘bulge ’ in the allies ’ defensive line-Allies comeback: skies cleared before Christmas so Allies ’ strong aircrafts pounded the invading army (US was known for powerful air forces since it fought Japan in pacific theater) - Allies pushed Germans back across the Rhine River-this battle was a soldier ’s fight without much direction from leaders-Guts, self-respect, loyalty to comrades prevailed over ideology-Allies won but; deaths: 19,000 American GI’s killed, 100,000 Germans died-marked the OFFICIAL BEGINNING FOR THE FALL OF THE GERMAN EMPIRE Wars in the Paci fic Theater (1941 -1944 ) 1) December 7th 1941: Japan attacks

Pearl Harbor-severely crippled the US pacific fleet-US had to use aircraft carriers and submarines after its battleship fleet crippled in Hawaii-Japan aimed to destroy US carrier fleet so that they could negotiate for peace Between: Allied forces repeatedly bombed and stormed Japanese -held territory, targeting tiny islands as well as the jungles of New Guinea and the Philippines-goal: secure airfields and supply bases that could serve as the launching points for future attacks 2) May 1942: Battle of the Coral Sea (Ended the peak of Japan) - both sides suffered humongous loses-definite win for the US-marked the first defeat for Japan 3) June 1942: Battle of Midway-TURNING POINT: US prevails, takes offensive for the first time-marked first major US victory against Japan-US destroyed four Japanese aircraft carriers 4) August 1942: Battle of Guadalcanal/Solomon Islands-allies took the first vital step in driving the Japanese back in the pacific theater-significance: the US stopped/prevented Japanese efforts from disrupting US supply routes to Australia and New Zealand-William Douglas Lansford participated in this combat 5) March 1943: Island Hopping Strategy -definition: the practice of skipping over heavily fortified islands in order to seize lightly defended locations that could support the next advance-turned the vast of pacific distances into an American ally, US used this to leapfrog across the pacific-practice: General Douglas MacAr thur ’s (US commander) troops first captured New Guinea, but found the heavily defended island of Rabaul to be formidable, so the fleets pushed westwards to first invade the less -defended islands-they eventually captured Rabaul successfully-why it worked out successfully: meanwhile MacArthur ’s troops practiced island hopping in the southwest pacific, there were central pacific campaigns in invading the Gilbert islands in November 1943; with two assaults on Japan, it crashed out 6) Jan/Feb 1944: Annihilating the Mariana Islands-KEY FOR THE INVASION OF MAINLAND JAPAN-Marianas were a particularly valuable asset since they were close enough to Japan for the US new B -29 bombs to bomb mainland
Japan 7) Feb-April 1945: Battle of Iwo Jima and Okinawa Battle of Iwo Jima-why?

It was a strategic air base located between the Mariana islands and Japan-Japanese preparation: carved out underground fortifications that turned the volcanic island into a death trap for invading US marines-the US planners only expected some brief campaigns but it happened to last over 5 weeks-Japanese commander General Kuribayashi concentrated forces in northern Iwo Jima islands with made the battle very bloody-names depicting the brutality of the combat: “The meat grinder ” (850 US marines died) and “bloody gorge ” (Japanese defenders made final stand) - US eventually took over-Symbol of Nationalism-February 23 1945, when US troops reached Mount Suribachi, they raised a small American flag but later returned to replace it with a larger flag-one of the most notable picture in WW2-William Douglas Lansford also participated in this, part of the field -intelligence unit-after this war, he worked as a Hollywood screenwriter and published books about history on W W2 and his experiences-Howard N.

Mclaughlin participated in this battle as a member of the repair section (heavy equipment) but later due to lack of soldiers on the frontline he also joined, part of the army-in his memoir, he wrote about the US marines ’ feelings toward the Japanese: “they neither liked or hated the Japs.
They killed them without anger or mercy.

To them they were part of the forces of evil that had to be destroyed ” Battle of Okinawa-April 1 1945, US tenth army arrived in Okinawa (last invasion before mainland Japan) - harsh conditions: heavy rains and rugged terrain-US overcame northern Okinawa by April 18 easily but overcoming the south was DIFFICULT because Japanese anchored their def enses at Shuri Castle with a series of well -defended high ridges-May 29 finally, US smashed down the Shuri Castle in southern Okinawa-March 26;

Kamikaze pilots: Japanese pilots intentionally crashed their planes into US aircraft carriers and other US battleships-This victory caused 1200 American deaths including the Tenth army ’s commander Lieutenant General Simon Buckner-Japanese: about 90,000 combatants died and 150,000 civilians died The End of WW2 (1944 -1945 ) 1.

THE EUROPEAN THEATER (officially ended on May 2nd 1945) Events that led to the end of war: (summary) Allies: “the only solution to this war is Germany ’s unconditional surrender ” 1) Operation Overlord (June 1944) and Battle of the Bulge (December 1944) - D-Day marked the beginning of Allied effort to liberate Western Europe from Hitler-After pushing eastward, allies fought battle of the bulge 2) USSR advancement from the east-After winning battle of Stalingrad and Kursk (southwest Russia) in 1943-1945, USSR reached Poland and conquered Berlin-they liberated concentration camps like Auschwitz; allies soldiers find the camps spine-chilling 3) April 25th 1944, American and USSR troops converge on Elbe River near Torgau-both knew the end of war was days away Why Hitler lost so badly/Consequences: - instead of surrendering when it was clear there was no turning back, he pulled grandfathers and children into the war - “fight to the last man ” - German soldiers however, surrendered-when he finally realized his failure, he committed suicide then German general signed contract with allies to express their unconditional surrender-May 8 1945 - V-E day (victory in Europe day) where allies celebrated their victory 2.

THE PACIFIC THEATER (officially ended on September 2) - May 1945: allies were still skeptical because Japan had never claimed their surrender so they might attack again-August 6, US atomic bombed Hiroshima-killed 140,000 people-USSR declares war on Japan and the Red Army takes Manchuria-Japan realizes an increase in enemy-led to their surrender-August 9, US atomic bombed Nagasaki-killed 70,000 people-August 14 Japanese then surrendered in the Potsdam conference-August 14: VJ Day for Americans

Sunnis supported Abu Bakr, a close companion of Muhammad, while Shi’as believed leadership should remain within Muhammad’s family, supporting Ali, his cousin and son-in-law.
Sunni Beliefs: Leadership should be chosen by consensus or election among the Muslim community; they form the majority of Muslims worldwide.
Shi’a Beliefs: Leadership (Imamate) should remain within Muhammad’s bloodline, with Ali and his descendants as rightful leaders.

Historical Implications: The conflict led to centuries of political and theological rivalry, with events like the assassination of Ali (661 CE) and the martyrdom of his son, Hussein, at Karbala (680 CE), which became pivotal moments in Shi’a identity and mourning traditions.
7-3 1. Islamic Religion and Law:
Islam emphasizes behavior and belief, integrating spiritual and societal duties as guided by the Qur'an and Shari'a law.
The Qur’an is viewed as divine and immutable, influencing all aspects of life including politics, law, economics, and ethics.
2. Political Structures:
Early Islamic governance faced challenges in aligning political authority with religious doctrine.
The caliph served as a temporal and spiritual leader, though disputes over succession led to divisions like the Sunni-Shi’a split.
3. Trade and Urban Prosperity:
The Islamic empire thrived on robust trade networks linking Africa, Asia, and Europe, supported by advanced maritime technology and banking systems.
Cities like Baghdad, Cairo, and Córdoba flourished as cultural and commercial hubs.
4. Society and Social Hierarchy:
Islamic society was relatively egalitarian for its time, though it practiced slavery and maintained gender hierarchies.
Women had rights like property ownership but were often subject to restrictive customs such as veiling and seclusion.
5. Cultural Achievements:
Philosophy and Science: Islamic scholars preserved and expanded upon Greek philosophy and sciences, making significant contributions in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine.
Literature: Persian and Arabic literature produced works like Ferdowsi’s The Book of Kings, Omar Khayyam’s Rubaiyat, and The Arabian Nights.

Art and Architecture: Islamic art blended geometric patterns, calligraphy, and arabesques, avoiding representational images of humans or the Prophet. Iconic structures include the Dome of the Rock and the Alhambra.
Sufism emerged as a mystical branch of Islam emphasizing personal connections with Allah through music, poetry, and dance, represented by poets like Rumi.
7. Historical Writing:
Historians like al-Mas’udi and Ibn Khaldun advanced historical methods, emphasizing critical analysis of sources and understanding historical dynamics.
8. Integration and Legacy:

Islamic civilization absorbed influences from Greek, Persian, and Indian traditions while creating enduring contributions in fields like science, literature, and architecture. Its intellectual legacy significantly impacted Europe during the medieval and Renaissance periods.

Mongol Origins and Rise:
Temuchin, later Genghis Khan unified Mongol tribes.
In 1206, Temuchin was elected Genghis Khan, starting the Mongol expansion.
The Mongol army was highly effective, using tactics like tireless flying columns, ambushes, and feigned retreats.
Mongol Empire and China:
The Mongols succeeded the Song as rulers of China in the late 13th century.
Genghis Khan died in 1227, and Mongol warriors completed the conquest of China by 1279, establishing the Yuan dynasty.
Kublai Khan, one of Genghis Khan's successors, completed the conquest of the Song dynasty and moved the capital to Dadu (modern-day Beijing).
Mongol Military Technology:
The Mongols encountered Chinese military inventions like the fire-lance, which evolved into more effective handguns and cannons by the end of the 13th century.
Mongol Empire Administration:
Genghis Khan set up a capital at Karakorum and initially prohibited fellow Mongols from sedentary occupations.
His successors adapted to conquered regions, and Mongol aristocrats began to take administrative positions.
After Genghis Khan's death, the unified empire divided into several khanates: the Khanate of Kipchak (Golden Horde)
Khanate of Chaghadai Khanate of Persia (Il-Khans) the Great Khanate.
Trade and Diplomacy:
Chinese ports exported a wide variety of goods: tea, silk, porcelain, precious stones, cotton, and tropical products

Canton was a major port. In 1245, Pope Innocent IV sent John Plano Carpini to the Mongol headquarters. Kuyuk Khan's reply to the Pope demanded submission and accused Christians of attacking the Mongols.
Mongol Rule in China:
Yuan rulers under Kublai Khan expanded sent Mongol armies into Vietnam and launching expeditions against Malay kingdoms in Java and Sumatra.
But conquests like in Vietnam and Japan were failures.
Initially, the Mongols struggled to govern China. they adopted Chinese political systems, used local talents, and retained some administrative structures.
Culturally, Mongols and Chinese remained separate:
Mongols followed their own laws, and while some converted to Buddhism, most commoners kept their traditional religions.
Decline of the Yuan Dynasty:
1340s. Excessive spending on conquests, tax issues, factionalism, corruption, and natural disasters
It was replaced by the Ming dynasty in 1369-1444.
The Mongols were powerful nomadic people:
Genghis Khan created an effective military system and used innovative tactics against enemies on the steppes.
After gaining power, the Mongols had trouble transitioning from nomadic to sedentary life, causing leadership instability.
Their expansion brought death and suffering, but also created the Pax Mongolica, a period of relative peace that facilitated trade across Eurasia.
The Ming Dynasty Expansion and Re-conquest:
The Ming dynasty expanded rule into Mongolia, Central Asia, and briefly reconquered Vietnam. fortified the northern frontier with the Great Wall had a tributary relationship with Korea.
Ming rulers reinstated traditional Confucian institutions, using civil service exams to select bureaucrats and dividing the empire for administration.
The Great Wall:
The Ming built part of the Great Wall was for protection against northern invasions..
Zheng He's Voyages:
In 1405, Emperor Yongle sent Zheng He on voyages with a large fleet reaching the east coast of Africa
Reasons for the voyages: trade expansion, alliance building, and power projection continued after his death

title: 14-1 An Age of Exploration and Expansion
points: Europeans weren't the first in Asian trade; Indian Ocean trade had thrived for centuries.
Vasco da Gama's voyage to India (late 15th century) is seen as a key moment, but Asian and
African trade networks were already well-established. The Portuguese keep the route in secret until the Dutch discover them later.
Muslim merchants had long dominated the spice trade, with trade routes connecting various regions.
Islam and the Spice Trade:
Muslim merchants had been involved in the spice trade for centuries, sailing from ports in Asia. By the 13th century, Islam had a presence in Southeast Asian islands and was spreading inland.
The spread of Islam in Southeast Asia was also influenced by new sultanates, like Malacca, founded in the early 15th century.
Spread of Islam in West Africa:
Muslim commercial and religious influence spread south across the Sahara to the Niger River
Valley. Muslim traders (Arabs and local converts) brought Islamic values, culture, and legal traditions, contributing to state formation (e.g., the kingdom of Mali).
The Great City of Timbuktu:
Became a major commercial hub for trans - Saharan trade, dealing in gold, salt, and other goods.
Had a well-developed social and economic system, with a significant Islamic scholarly community.
Leo Africanus described its wealth, including trade in precious goods and the use of currency (such as cowrie shells and gold).
Motives for European Expansion:
“God, Gold, and Glory”. Missionary efforts to spread Christianity, desire for wealth (gold, spices), and pursuit of fame and national glory.
Technological advancements (e.g., better ships, navigational tools like the compass and astrolabe) enabled these voyages.
14-2 The Portuguese Maritime Empire:
Portuguese Exploration Start:
Began exploring the western coast of Africa under Prince Henry the Navigator, aiming for gold trade, weakening Muslim states, and spreading Christianity.
Established a school for navigators and built forts along the African coast.
Voyages to India:
Vasco da Gama's voyage to India (1497 - 1499) was a milestone. He reached the port of Calicut, and his voyage was sponsored to break the Muslim monopoly on the spice trade.
Subsequent Portuguese efforts included establishing trade posts and forts, like at Malacca, to control trade routes.
Success and Challenges:
Succeeded initially due to a strong navy, advanced ships, and cannon technology.
Faced challenges from Muslim rivals and later European competitors (e.g., Spain, England,
Netherlands). Struggled to maintain dominance long-term due to over-extension, high costs, and competition.
Dividing Up the Spoils of Exploration:
Portugal and Spain signed the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) to divide newly discovered territories.
The treaty set a line of demarcation, giving most of the Americas to Spain and areas east (including
Africa and Asia) to Portugal, but later disputes arose over exact boundaries. This leads to several violations of the treaty in the future.

title: European Powers in the Americas
points: Spanish Exploration and Conquest:
Christopher Columbus (Italian sailing for Spain) reached the Americas in 1492, mistakenly believing he had reached Asia.

Spanish conquistadors (e.g., Herná n Corté s in Mexico, Francisco Pizarro in Peru) conquered major indigenous empires (Aztec, Inca) using superior weapons, alliances with rival groups, and the spread of European diseases.
Established a large colonial empire in the Americas, including areas like Mexico, Central
America, and much of South America.
Portuguese in Brazil:

Geography and Civilization Development
The Fertile Crescent extends from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea, encompassing Mesopotamia.
Sumer emerged around 3300 B.C. in southeastern Mesopotamia.
The region's rivers were crucial for agriculture but posed challenges due to frequent flooding, as depicted in The Epic of Gilgamesh.
Survival and Cooperation Communities collaborated to manage floods and ensure agricultural success.
Leadership often came from temple priests or royal officials who organized dike and irrigation system construction.
Urban Development in Sumer
Sumerians thrived by utilizing clay for construction, creating sun-dried bricks for cities like Ur and Uruk.
Trade routes facilitated the exchange of goods; the Sumerians possibly invented the wheel.
Structure of Sumerian Society

Governance evolved from military leaders to hereditary rulers responsible for:
City maintenance Law enforcement
Religious ceremonies Social Hierarchy:
Highest class: Ruling family, high officials, priests
Middle class: Lesser priests, scribes, merchants, artisans

Religious Practices in Sumer

Akkadians Babylonians Assyrians

Dividing time into 60 minutes
Circles into 360 degrees

The Fertile Crescent, a region in the Middle East known for its rich soils, was home to several early civilizations. This area became a crossroads for nomadic herders, traders, and invaders, leading to a blend of cultures and ideas.
Fertile Crescent: Piece of rich land around Mesopotamia
Hierarchy: How members of a system are ranked according to authority, etc. Ziggurat: Ancient Mesopotamian temples
The Fertile Crescent extends from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea, encompassing Mesopotamia, which lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
Around 3300 B.C., Sumer emerged in southeastern Mesopotamia. The region's rivers were crucial for agriculture but also posed challenges due to frequent flooding, as depicted in The Epic of Gilgamesh.

Survival and Cooperation To manage the floods and ensure agricultural success, communities had to collaborate. Leadership often came from temple priests or royal officials who organized efforts to build dikes and irrigation systems. This cooperation was essential for survival in the face of natural disasters.

Despite limited natural resources, the Sumerians thrived by utilizing clay for construction. They created sun-dried bricks to build cities like Ur and Uruk. Trade routes facilitated the exchange of goods, and the Sumerians may have invented the wheel, enhancing transportation and commerce.

By 2500 B.C., Sumer consisted of at least 12 city-states, often in conflict over resources. Governance evolved from military leaders to hereditary rulers responsible for city maintenance, law enforcement, and religious ceremonies. Sumerian society was hierarchical:

Sumerians were polytheistic, worshiping many gods who influenced all aspects of life. They built ziggurats for religious ceremonies and believed in an afterlife characterized by a grim underworld. Rituals were performed to appease the gods, ensuring the city's prosperity.

Development of Writing By 3200 B.C., Sumerians developed cuneiform, the earliest known writing system, which evolved from pictographs. This writing allowed for the recording of economic transactions, myths, and laws. Scribes underwent rigorous training, and their skills were essential for administration and communication.

Lasting Legacy of Sumer Despite the eventual conquest of Sumer by other civilizations, its innovations in writing, mathematics, and astronomy had a lasting impact. Sumerian knowledge influenced later cultures, including the Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians, who adapted cuneiform for their languages. Sumerians established a base for mathematics, dividing time into 60 minutes and circles into 360 degrees, which persists today.

Conclusion The Sumerians left a profound legacy that shaped the development of subsequent civilizations in the region and beyond. Their contributions to writing, governance, and science laid the groundwork for future advancements in human history.

title: Invades, Traders, and Empire Builders
points: Key Terms, People, and Places
Sargon: Ruler of Akkad who built the first empire.
Hammurabi: King of Babylon known for codifying laws.
Zoroaster: Persian thinker who introduced a monotheistic religion.
Barter Economy: System of exchange where goods and services are traded directly.
Money Economy: System where goods and services are paid for with currency.
Civil Law: Laws governing private rights and matters.
Criminal Law: Laws dealing with offenses against others.
Alphabet: Writing system where symbols represent sounds.
First Empires Arise in Mesopotamia

Throughout history, nomadic peoples and warriors invaded the Fertile Crescent, leading to the establishment of powerful empires. Sargon of Akkad, around 2300 B.C., created the first known empire by conquering Sumerian city-states and appointing local rulers. However, his empire fell apart after his death due to subsequent invasions.

Hammurabi and Babylon Hammurabi, king of Babylon around 1790 B.C., revived Sumerian city-states and imposed unity over the region. His most notable achievement was Hammurabi's Code, a comprehensive set of laws carved on a stone pillar, which aimed to codify legal principles for the empire.

Hammurabi’s Code Hammurabi's Code included civil law, addressing private rights such as business contracts, property inheritance, and marriage. It aimed to protect the powerless, including women and slaves, allowing women to own property and outlining their rights in marriage.

The code also established criminal law, detailing specific punishments for offenses to promote social order. Punishments often followed the principle of "an eye for an eye," which, while harsh by modern standards, provided a more structured legal system than personal vengeance.
Other Accomplishments of Hammurabi
Besides his legal contributions, Hammurabi improved irrigation systems, organized a strong army, and promoted religious unity by elevating the worship of Marduk, Babylon's chief god.
Conquests Bring New Empires and Ideas

Subsequent empires, such as the Hittites and Assyrians, brought new technologies and ideas to the region. The Hittites, around 1400 B.C., introduced ironworking, leading to stronger tools and weapons, which contributed to their military success.

Assyrian Expansion The Assyrians, known for their fierce warrior culture, expanded their empire by 1100 B.C. They established a well-ordered society, built impressive palaces, and created one of the first libraries in Nineveh, preserving cuneiform tablets that provide insights into ancient life.
Nebuchadnezzar and the Revival of Babylon

After the fall of the Assyrians, Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon, enhancing its defenses and infrastructure. He constructed the famous Ishtar Gate and possibly the Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, to please his wife.

The Persian Empire In 539 B.C., Babylon fell to the Persians under Cyrus the Great, who established the largest empire of the time. The Persian Empire was characterized by tolerance and respect for the customs of conquered peoples.

Darius I's Reforms Darius I unified the empire by dividing it into provinces (satrapies) governed by satraps. He implemented a single code of laws, improved communication through roads, and introduced a standardized system of weights and measures, facilitating trade.
Darius encouraged the use of coins, transitioning from a barter economy to a money economy, which simplified trade and economic transactions.
Zoroastrianism Zoroaster's teachings introduced a dualistic worldview, emphasizing the struggle between good (Ahura Mazda) and evil (Ahriman), influencing later religions like Christianity and Islam.
Contributions of Phoenician Traders

While empires rose and fell, the Phoenicians, known for their maritime trade, established colonies and spread their culture throughout the Mediterranean. They were skilled manufacturers, producing glass and the famous Tyrian purple dye.
They also developed the early alphabets (22 consonant sounds)

title: Kingdom on the Nile Geography's Influence on Egypt
points: Herodotus, an ancient Greek historian, stated that "Egypt is wholly the gift of the Nile." The Nile provided a narrow band of fertile land, known as the "Black Land," surrounded by the inhospitable "Red Land" desert. This geography limited settlement areas but also protected Egypt from invasions.
Farming villages thrived along the Nile.
Farmers grew crops like wheat and flax, benefiting from the fertile soil.
Yearly Floods and Their Benefits
The Nile's annual floods, caused by rains in Ethiopia and central Africa, were crucial for agriculture. The floods soaked the land and deposited rich silt, enhancing soil fertility.
Cooperation was necessary to manage the floods.
Early governments built dikes, reservoirs, and irrigation systems to control water flow.

Unification of Egypt Ancient Egypt was divided into Upper Egypt (south) and Lower Egypt (north). Around 3100 B.C., King Menes united these regions, establishing Memphis as the first capital. The Nile served as a highway for trade and communication, facilitating the emergence of one of the world's first unified states.
Egyptian merchants utilized the Nile for trade, exchanging goods with regions across Africa, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean.
Egyptian Periods Egypt's history is divided into three main periods: the Old Kingdom (2575 B.C.-2130 B.C.), the Middle Kingdom (1938 B.C.-1630 B.C.), and the New Kingdom (1539 B.C.-1075 B.C.).
Government Structure in the Old Kingdom
During the Old Kingdom, pharaohs established a centralized government. They were viewed as gods and held absolute power, supported by a bureaucracy that managed various aspects of governance.
Viziers supervised government operations.
Departments managed tax collection, farming, and irrigation.
Pyramids and Afterlife Beliefs

Pharaohs built necropolises and pyramids, such as the Great Pyramids at Giza, as tombs for the afterlife. These structures were seen as eternal homes for the deceased, reflecting the Egyptians' belief in an afterlife.
Pyramids required extensive resources and labor.
Construction involved thousands of workers and took decades to complete.
The Middle Kingdom's Challenges
The Middle Kingdom faced power struggles, crop failures, and corruption. Despite these challenges, strong rulers initiated large drainage projects to create arable land and expanded trade contacts.
The Hyksos invaded around 1700 B.C., introducing new military technologies.
Egyptians adopted some Hyksos customs, leading to cultural exchange.
The New Kingdom and Expansion

The New Kingdom marked a period of expansion and conquest, with pharaohs like Hatshepsut and Thutmose III extending Egypt's borders. Hatshepsut was notable as Egypt's first female ruler, promoting trade and building monumental structures.
Ramses II, another significant pharaoh, engaged in military campaigns and signed a peace treaty with the Hittites.
Egypt's empire reached its height around 1450 B.C., encompassing parts of Syria and the Euphrates River.

Decline of Egyptian Power After 1100 B.C., Egypt's power began to decline due to invasions by the Assyrians and Persians. The last Egyptian dynasty ended in 332 B.C. with Greek control, followed by Roman conquest in 30 B.C.
