title: Background to the Reformation
points: Northern Europeans faced life uncertainty. Fixed medieval economies shifted to urban, market-based ones with unequal wealth distribution.
Renaissance humanist ideas spread via the printing press. Ideas like classical education and social reform took root, leading people to question the Church.

Church abuses were rife. Popes engaged in political power struggles, led lavish lives, and increased service fees. Some clergy sold indulgences, which were originally for good deeds but by the late 1400s could be bought with money.
Early revolts against the Church occurred. John Wycliffe in 1300s England and Jan Hus in what's now the Czech Republic protested Church practices.

title: Martin Luther: Catalyst of Change
points: In 1517, Johann Tetzel's sale of indulgences to fund St. Peter's Cathedral rebuilding enraged Luther. Tetzel claimed indulgences guaranteed heaven for buyers and their dead relatives.
Luther wrote the 95 Theses against indulgences. Argued they had no basis in the Bible, the pope had no authority over purgatory, and salvation was through faith.
Copies of the 95 Theses spread rapidly across Europe, sparking debate. Luther refused to recant when the Church demanded it.
Luther developed radical doctrines. Urged Christians to reject Rome's authority, believed the Church could be reformed by secular authorities.
In 1521, Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther. Emperor Charles V summoned him to the Diet of Worms. Luther refused to give up his writings, was declared an outlaw.
Luther's Teachings Salvation by faith alone. All Christians had equal access to God through faith and the Bible.
Rejected some sacraments. Believed rituals couldn't erase sin; only God could.
Bible as the sole source of truth. Luther translated parts of the Bible into German and wanted everyone to be able to read it.
Simplified church practices. Banned indulgences, confession, pilgrimages, and prayers to saints. Simplified the mass and emphasized sermons. Allowed clergy to marry.
Luther's Ideas Spread Printing presses spread Luther's writings in Germany and Scandinavia.
Many clergy saw his reforms as a solution to Church corruption.
Some German princes embraced Lutheranism for self-serving reasons. To break free from Church and imperial rule, seize Church property, or due to national loyalty.

The Peasants' Revolt in 1524 was inspired by Luther's ideas. Peasants hoped for social and economic change, like an end to serfdom. Luther denounced the revolt as it grew violent, and nobles suppressed it.
The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed German princes to choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism. Most northern states chose Lutheranism, southern states remained Catholic.
Switzerland's Reformation Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich stressed the importance of the Bible and rejected elaborate rituals.
John Calvin, born in France, published a book in 1536. Set forth his beliefs, including predestination (God had long ago determined who would be saved).
In 1541, Calvin led Geneva. Set up a theocracy run by church leaders. Calvinists emphasized hard work, discipline, thrift, honesty, and morality.
Calvinism spread across Europe. It led to religious wars in Germany, France, the Netherlands, England, and Scotland.

title: An Explosion of Protestant Sects
points: As the Reformation continued, numerous new Protestant sects emerged.
Anabaptists were a radical group. Rejected infant baptism, arguing infants were too young to understand the Christian faith.
Some Anabaptist sects sought social change. Wanted to abolish private property or speed up God's judgment day.
Most Anabaptists were peaceful. Called for religious toleration and separation of church and state. Influenced Protestant thinking; Baptists, Mennonites, and Amish trace their roots to them.
The English Reformation In the 1300s, John Wycliffe called for Church reform in England. By the 1520s, some clergy explored Protestant ideas.
Henry VIII initially opposed Protestantism. The pope gave him the title "Defender of the Faith" for denouncing Luther.
In 1527, Henry wanted an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He wanted to marry Anne Boleyn to have a male heir. The pope refused, not wanting to offend Charles V.
Henry broke with the Church. Guided by Thomas Cromwell, Parliament passed laws taking the English church from papal control. Henry appointed Thomas Cranmer as archbishop.
In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, making Henry the head of the Church of England. Loyal Catholics who refused to accept it, like Sir Thomas More, were executed.
Henry closed Catholic convents and monasteries between 1536-1540. Confiscated their lands and wealth, and granted some to nobles to secure support for the Anglican Church.
After Henry's death, Edward VI became king. He and his advisors were Protestants. Parliament passed laws for Protestant reforms, and Cranmer drew up the Protestant Book of Common Prayer.
Mary Tudor became queen after Edward's death. She tried to restore Catholicism. Hundreds of Protestants, including Cranmer, were burned at the stake.

Elizabeth I became queen in 1558. Her Elizabethan Settlement was a compromise between Protestant and Catholic practices. Preserved Catholic rituals, reaffirmed the monarch's spiritual authority, and restored a version of the Book of Common Prayer.
The Catholic Reformation Led by Pope Paul III, the Catholic Reformation aimed to revive the Church's moral authority and counter the Protestant tide.
The Council of Trent, called in 1545, met for almost 20 years. Reaffirmed traditional Catholic views, declared salvation through faith and good works, and took steps to end Church abuses.
Pope Paul strengthened the Inquisition. It used secret testimony, torture, and execution to fight Protestantism and created the Index of Forbidden Books.

In 1540, the Jesuits (Society of Jesus) were founded by Ignatius of Loyola. They had strict spiritual and moral discipline, and their members became advisors to Catholic rulers, set up schools, and spread the Catholic faith worldwide.
Teresa of Avila, a Spanish nun, reformed convents and monasteries. Her spiritual writings were important, and she was canonized.
By 1600, the Catholic Reformation had reduced Church abuses, brought back some Protestant converts, but Protestantism still had a major foothold in Europe.
Widespread Persecution During the Reformation, both Catholics and Protestants persecuted radical sects, witches, and Jews.
Witch hunts occurred between 1450-1750. Tens of thousands of mostly women were accused of being witches, seen as anti-Christian. Persecution declined with the end of religious wars.

Jews faced increasing restrictions. Venice ordered them to live in ghettos in 1516. Luther called for their expulsion when they didn't convert. Popes and emperors also imposed restrictions, leading many Jews to migrate.

title: Changing Views of the Universe
points: Until the mid-1500s, Europeans believed in the Earth-centered universe theory of Ptolemy and Aristotle, which was supported by the Church.
In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. Proposed a heliocentric (sun-centered) model of the universe.
Most experts rejected Copernicus's theory. It challenged classical and religious teachings.
Tycho Brahe set up an observatory. His observations provided evidence for Copernicus's theory.
Johannes Kepler used Brahe's data. Calculated that planets move in elliptical orbits, supporting Copernicus's heliocentric view.

Galileo Galilei built a telescope. Observed Jupiter's moons, which supported the heliocentric view. His discoveries were opposed by scholars and condemned by the Church. He was tried and placed under house arrest.
A New Scientific Method In the early 1600s, a new scientific method emerged. Based on observation and experimentation.
Francis Bacon stressed experimentation and observation. Wanted science to improve people's lives through practical technologies.
René Descartes emphasized human reasoning. His famous statement was "I think, therefore I am."
The scientific method involved collecting and measuring data. Proposing a hypothesis, testing it, and repeating the process.

title: Breakthroughs in Medicine and Chemistry
points: In medicine, Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body in 1543. It was the first accurate study of human anatomy.
Ambroise Paré developed new surgical techniques and an anti-infection ointment.
William Harvey described blood circulation in the early 1600s.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek perfected the microscope. First to see cells and microorganisms.
In chemistry, alchemy was transformed. Robert Boyle refined the view of chemicals. Distinguished between elements and compounds, and explained the behavior of gases.

title: Isaac Newton Links the Sciences
points: Isaac Newton saw an apple fall. Wondered if the same force controlled the planets' movement.
He developed the theory of gravity. Showed that a single force keeps planets in orbit.
In 1687, Newton published a book explaining the law of gravity. Argued nature follows uniform laws.
Newton's laws held for over 200 years. Calculus, developed in part by Newton, is still used today.

Music and dance used in ceremonies.
Religion and mythology shown in sculpture and murals.

title: – The Search for Spices
points: Motivations for Exploration
Europeans wanted to control trade, especially the spice trade from Asia
Spices were used to preserve food, add flavor, make perfumes and medicine
Arab and Italian merchants controlled trade routes; Europeans wanted direct access
Curiosity from the Renaissance inspired exploration
Important Places and People
Moluccas: Spice Islands in Indonesia

Portuguese explorer who reached India by sailing around Africa

1415: Seized Ceuta in North Africa
1488: Bartholomeu Dias reached Cape of Good Hope
1497: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, India and started a Portuguese trading empire

Sponsored by King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of spain
Backed by Spain in 1492, found Caribbean islands

Found the Strait of Magellan, crossed the Pacific Ocean
Killed in the Philippines 1522: Survivors circumnavigated the globe Key Review Questions (14.1) 1.

To gain direct access to the spice trade and avoid Arab and Italian middlemen.
2. What impact did Prince Henry and Vasco da Gama have on exploration?
3. How did the Treaty of Tordesillas affect global exploration?
It divided the world between Spain and Portugal, encouraging both to build global empires.
伽马等探险家推动了非洲沿海的探索并建立了通往印度的航线。哥 伦布向西航行发现了新大陆，引发了西班牙和葡萄牙的殖民竞争。教皇划定了 “教皇子午 线”，随后签订《托尔德西利亚斯条约》，使世界被这两个国家划分，从而开启了全球殖民 的新时代。 14.2 – Turbulent Centuries in Africa (probably not in the test)

title: Why or why not?
points: 中文重点 (Chinese Summary): 宗教改革: 对教会腐败的抗议，路德（95条）与加尔文为关键人物。 路德宗: 信仰得救、《圣经》最高、牧师可结婚。 加尔文主义: 预定论、神权政治、严格生活方式。 影响: 印刷术推动改革；《奥格斯堡和约》支持信仰自由。 Section 13.3: The Protestant Reformation Background to the Reformation Northern Europeans faced life uncertainty.
Fixed medieval economies shifted to urban, market-based ones with unequal wealth distribution.
Renaissance humanist ideas spread via the printing press.
Ideas like classical education and social reform took root, leading people to question the Church.
Church abuses were rife. Popes engaged in political power struggles, led lavish lives, and increased service fees.
Some clergy sold indulgences, which were originally for good deeds but by the late 1400s could be bought with money.
Early revolts against the Church occurred.
John Wycliffe in 1300s England and Jan Hus in what's now the Czech Republic protested Church practices.
Martin Luther: Catalyst of Change In 1517, Johann Tetzel's sale of indulgences to fund St. Peter's Cathedral rebuilding enraged Luther.
Tetzel claimed indulgences guaranteed heaven for buyers and their dead relatives.
Luther wrote the 95 Theses against indulgences.
Argued they had no basis in the Bible, the pope had no authority over purgatory, and salvation was through faith.
Copies of the 95 Theses spread rapidly across Europe, sparking debate.
Luther refused to recant when the Church demanded it.
Luther developed radical doctrines.
Urged Christians to reject Rome's authority, believed the Church could be reformed by secular authorities.
In 1521, Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther.
Emperor Charles V summoned him to the Diet of Worms.
Luther refused to give up his writings, was declared an outlaw.
Luther's Teachings Salvation by faith alone.
All Christians had equal access to God through faith and the Bible.
Rejected some sacraments. Believed rituals couldn't erase sin; only God could.
Bible as the sole source of truth.
Luther translated parts of the Bible into German and wanted everyone to be able to read it.
Simplified church practices.
Banned indulgences, confession, pilgrimages, and prayers to saints.
Simplified the mass and emphasized sermons.
Allowed clergy to marry. Luther's Ideas Spread Printing presses spread Luther's writings in Germany and Scandinavia.
Some German princes embraced Lutheranism for self-serving reasons.
To break free from Church and imperial rule, seize Church property, or due to national loyalty.
The Peasants' Revolt in 1524 was inspired by Luther's ideas.
Peasants hoped for social and economic change, like an end to serfdom.
Luther denounced the revolt as it grew violent, and nobles suppressed it.
The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed German princes to choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism.
Most northern states chose Lutheranism, southern states remained Catholic.
Switzerland's Reformation Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich stressed the importance of the Bible and rejected elaborate rituals.
John Calvin, born in France, published a book in 1536.
Set forth his beliefs, including predestination (God had long ago determined who would be saved).
In 1541, Calvin led Geneva.
Set up a theocracy run by church leaders.
Calvinists emphasized hard work, discipline, thrift, honesty, and morality.
Calvinism spread across Europe.
It led to religious wars in Germany, France, the Netherlands, England, and Scotland.
Section 13.4: Reformation Ideas Spread An Explosion of Protestant Sects As the Reformation continued, numerous new Protestant sects emerged.
Anabaptists were a radical group.
Rejected infant baptism, arguing infants were too young to understand the Christian faith.
Some Anabaptist sects sought social change.
Wanted to abolish private property or speed up God's judgment day.
Most Anabaptists were peaceful.
Called for religious toleration and separation of church and state.
Influenced Protestant thinking; Baptists, Mennonites, and Amish trace their roots to them.
The English Reformation In the 1300s, John Wycliffe called for Church reform in England.
By the 1520s, some clergy explored Protestant ideas.
Henry VIII initially opposed Protestantism.
The pope gave him the title "Defender of the Faith" for denouncing Luther.
In 1527, Henry wanted an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
He wanted to marry Anne Boleyn to have a male heir.
The pope refused, not wanting to offend Charles V.
Henry broke with the Church.
Guided by Thomas Cromwell, Parliament passed laws taking the English church from papal control.
Henry appointed Thomas Cranmer as archbishop.
In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, making Henry the head of the Church of England.
Loyal Catholics who refused to accept it, like Sir Thomas More, were executed.
Henry closed Catholic convents and monasteries between 1536-1540.
Confiscated their lands and wealth, and granted some to nobles to secure support for the Anglican Church.
After Henry's death, Edward VI became king.
He and his advisors were Protestants.
Parliament passed laws for Protestant reforms, and Cranmer drew up the Protestant Book of Common Prayer.
Mary Tudor became queen after Edward's death.
She tried to restore Catholicism.
Hundreds of Protestants, including Cranmer, were burned at the stake.
Elizabeth I became queen in 1558.
Her Elizabethan Settlement was a compromise between Protestant and Catholic practices.
Preserved Catholic rituals, reaffirmed the monarch's spiritual authority, and restored a version of the Book of Common Prayer.
The Catholic Reformation Led by Pope Paul III, the Catholic Reformation aimed to revive the Church's moral authority and counter the Protestant tide.
The Council of Trent, called in 1545, met for almost 20 years.
Reaffirmed traditional Catholic views, declared salvation through faith and good works, and took steps to end Church abuses.
Pope Paul strengthened the Inquisition.
It used secret testimony, torture, and execution to fight Protestantism and created the Index of Forbidden Books.
In 1540, the Jesuits (Society of Jesus) were founded by Ignatius of Loyola.
They had strict spiritual and moral discipline, and their members became advisors to Catholic rulers, set up schools, and spread the Catholic faith worldwide.
Teresa of Avila, a Spanish nun, reformed convents and monasteries.
Her spiritual writings were important, and she was canonized.
Widespread Persecution During the Reformation, both Catholics and Protestants persecuted radical sects, witches, and Jews.
Witch hunts occurred between 1450-1750.
Tens of thousands of mostly women were accused of being witches, seen as anti-Christian.
Persecution declined with the end of religious wars.
Jews faced increasing restrictions.
Venice ordered them to live in ghettos in 1516.
Luther called for their expulsion when they didn't convert.
Popes and emperors also imposed restrictions, leading many Jews to migrate.

Section 13.5: The Scientific Revolution Changing Views of the Universe Until the mid-1500s, Europeans believed in the Earth-centered universe theory of Ptolemy and Aristotle, which was supported by the Church.
In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres.
Proposed a heliocentric (sun-centered) model of the universe.
Most experts rejected Copernicus's theory.
It challenged classical and religious teachings.
Tycho Brahe set up an observatory.
His observations provided evidence for Copernicus's theory.
Johannes Kepler used Brahe's data.
Calculated that planets move in elliptical orbits, supporting Copernicus's heliocentric view.
Galileo Galilei built a telescope.
Observed Jupiter's moons, which supported the heliocentric view.
His discoveries were opposed by scholars and condemned by the Church.
He was tried and placed under house arrest.
A New Scientific Method In the early 1600s, a new scientific method emerged.
Based on observation and experimentation.
Francis Bacon stressed experimentation and observation.
Wanted science to improve people's lives through practical technologies.
René Descartes emphasized human reasoning.
His famous statement was "I think, therefore I am." The scientific method involved collecting and measuring data.
Proposing a hypothesis, testing it, and repeating the process.
Breakthroughs in Medicine and Chemistry In medicine, Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body in 1543.
It was the first accurate study of human anatomy.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek perfected the microscope.
First to see cells and microorganisms.
In chemistry, alchemy was transformed.
Robert Boyle refined the view of chemicals.
Distinguished between elements and compounds, and explained the behavior of gases.
Isaac Newton Links the Sciences Isaac Newton saw an apple fall.
Wondered if the same force controlled the planets' movement.
He developed the theory of gravity.
Showed that a single force keeps planets in orbit.
In 1687, Newton published a book explaining the law of gravity.
Argued nature follows uniform laws.
Newton's laws held for over 200 years.
Calculus, developed in part by Newton, is still used today.

title: What did he accomplish?
points: Constantine rebuilt the Greek city of Byzantium then renamed it after himself—Constantinople.
Through this time, roads fanned out and the Eastern Roman Empire became known as the Byzantine Empire.
Q2. How did Constantinople become a rich and powerful city?
The vital center and capital of the empire was Constantinople, located on the shore of the Bosporus, a strait that links the Mediterranean and Black seas.
Constantinople had an excellent harbor and was guarded on three sides by water as well as sea walls on a high land to bolster its defenses.

title: Q3. What are Justinian’s accomplishments?
points: The Byzantine Empire reached to its peak under the rule of the emperor Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565.
Justinian launched a construction project to restore the Byzantine empire back to its past glories.

He created countless cities, buildings, and churches including the Hagia Sophia (Meaning “Holy Wisdom”, topped with a spherical-shaped dome and serves as a cathedral of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, Roman Christian cathedral, and Islamic Mosque).
He established the firm foundations of a single faith and preserved laws in the Code of Justinian that unified the empire.
Q4. How did Eastern and Western churches differ?
In Western churches, Rome was the main city.
The pope claimed reign after all Christians and spoke Latin as their main language.
Christmas was a major holiday.
In Eastern Churches, Constantinople was the main city.
The Byzantine Emperor controlled church affairs and appointed the patriarch.
Byzantine Christians rejected the pope’s authority and clergies were allowed to marry.
They spoke Greek and viewed Easter as a more important holiday.

title: Q5. What Was the Great Schism?
points: The differences between religious beliefs, practices, and use of icons provoked a schism, or split, between the Eastern and Western Christianity, known as the Great Schism.
The Eastern Byzantine church became known as the Greek Orthodox Church, while the Western church became known as the Roman Catholic Church.
They treated each other as rivals.
Q6. What Factors Led to the Fall of the Byzantine Empire?
Struggles over succession, court intrigues, and constant wars undermined the empire’s strength.
THE Byzantine’s emperor called the Western help to fight the Seljuks, whose attacks blacked the pilgrimage routes to Jerusalem, resulting in the first crusade.
During the next crusades, trade sparked violence between the Byzantine Empire and Venice, a city-state in northern Italy.
Venetian merchants persuaded soldiers to attack Constantinople in the fourth crusade.
The crusaders burned and plunged the city, controlling the Byzantine trade, draining the empire’s wealth.
10.1 The Rise of Islam Introduction to Islam Islam emerged in the Arabian Peninsula, primarily in the A.D.
500s, amidst a desert environment inhabited by various Arab tribes.
The region was characterized by: Nomadic herders known as Bedouins who sought seasonal pastures for their livestock.
Muhammad's Early Life Muhammad was born in Mecca around A.D.
570, a significant market town and pilgrimage center.
Key points about his early life include: Mecca was a hub for caravan routes and housed the Kaaba, an ancient temple for pagan worship.
Muhammad Becomes God's Messenger At around 40, Muhammad experienced a spiritual awakening while meditating in a cave.
Significant aspects include: He heard the angel Gabriel calling him to be God's messenger, which initially terrified him.
The Hijra: A Turning Point In 622, Muhammad and his followers fled Mecca for Yathrib (later Medina) due to threats against their lives.
Important details include: The hijra marked the beginning of the Muslim calendar.
Teachings of Islam Islam is a monotheistic faith, sharing similarities with Judaism and Christianity.
Key teachings include: The Quran is the sacred text, emphasizing God's power and compassion.
Muslims Study the Quran The Quran is viewed as the direct word of God, providing guidance on ethical standards and life.
Key points include: It emphasizes honesty, generosity, and social justice.

Five Pillars of Islam Observant Muslims adhere to the Five Pillars of Islam, which are essential duties: Declaration of Faith: The shahada states, "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the messenger of God." Daily Prayer: Muslims pray five times a day facing Mecca, often gathering in mosques.
Jihad and the People of the Book Jihad represents the struggle in God's service, which can be personal or communal.
Key points include: Muslims, Jews, and Christians are considered "People of the Book," sharing a belief in one God.
Islamic Law and Women's Rights Islamic law, or Sharia, governs various aspects of life, integrating religious principles into legal frameworks.
Important aspects include: Sharia regulates moral conduct, family life, and business practices.
Impact of Islam on Women Islam improved the status of women compared to pre-Islamic society, but challenges remained.
The Quran's Structure and Teachings The Quran consists of 114 suras (chapters) and is considered the word of God.
Key teachings include: Righteousness is defined by belief in God and good deeds, including charity and prayer.
Key Vocabulary: Bedouins- Nomadic herders who moved through the dessert to reach seasonal pasture lands for their herds.
Mecca- Market town at the crossroad of several caravan routes in Saudi Arabia and a pilgrimage center.

Holy city of Islam Yathrib- A significant city in the history of Islam that served as a refuge for Muhammad and his followers Hijra- Muhammad’s sacred journey to Yathrib Medina- The new name for Yathrib or “City of Prophet” Kaaba- Temple built by Abraham to worship one true God, later used to worship Allah as the holy temple Quran- Sacred text of Islam, teaches that God is all powerful and compassionate Mosque- House of worship where Muslims gather and pray Hajj- Pilgrimage to Mecca Jihad- Struggle in God’s service Sharia
Body of law that includes interpretations of the Quran Q1.
What messages, or teachings, did Muhammad spread though Islam?
Muhammad rejected traditional gods and left Mecca with his followers to Yathrib on a sacred journey called hijra.
He dedicated the temple of Kaaba to Allah and practiced monotheistic.
Muslims were required to study the Quan, which contains the sacred word of God, as revealed to Muhammad.
It teaches about God’s will and provides a guide to life.
Its standards emphasize honesty, generosity, and social justice, such as setting harsh punishments to those who commit crime.
How did Muhammad become the prophet of Islam?
Muhammad was known for his honesty in business and was a devoted husband father.
He was troubled by the moral ills of society, especially greed.
He was about 40 when he heard the voice of voice of the angel Gabriel calling him to become the messenger of God.
Muhammad was confused and terrified, but his wife encouraged him to accept the call.
Muhammad devoted his life to spreading Islam.

title: What are the duties required of Muslims?
points: All Muslims preform the 5 pillars of Islam.
The first is to make a declaration of faith, the second is to pray 5 times daily in a house of worship called mosque.
The third is to give charity to the poor, or Almsgiving, and the third is Fasting between dawn and sunset in the month of Ramadan.
Lastly, the fifth is to make the hajji, or pilgrimage to Mecca.
Additionally, Jihad is a personal duty for Islam, or struggle in God’s service.

title: How did Islam Affect Women?
points: Arab women had limited rights.
However, Islam extended rights and protection to women by affirming the spiritual equality of all Muslims.
The Quan prohibited the killing of daughters, granted women an inheritance, allowed women to reject a marriage offer as well as equal education to study the Quran.
Sill, women’s life and dressing varied to region and class, while still having less statis than men.

10.2 Building a Muslim Empire The Death of Muhammad The death of Muhammad caused significant grief among his followers, raising concerns about the future of the Muslim community without his leadership.
Early Challenges to Islam After Muhammad's death, there was no designated successor, leading to uncertainty.
Early Victories Under the first four caliphs, Muslims achieved significant victories against the Byzantine and Persian empires.
Divisions Emerge Within Islam Disagreements over leadership after Muhammad's death led to the emergence of Sunni and Shiite branches of Islam.
The Dome of the Rock The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem is significant as it marks the site where Muslims believe Muhammad ascended to heaven.
Sufism Sufis emerged as a mystical tradition within Islam, focusing on personal communion with God through various practices.
Umayyad Caliphs Build an Empire After Ali's death, the Umayyad dynasty established a caliphate that expanded the Muslim empire significantly.
Reasons for Muslim Success Weakness of the Byzantine and Persian empires due to prolonged conflicts.
Conquered People Are Treated Fairly Muslim leaders imposed a tax on non-Muslims but allowed them to practice their religions, fostering a diverse society.
Decline of the Umayyad Caliphate As the Umayyad dynasty expanded, it faced internal and external challenges that led to its decline.
Harun al-Rashid Caliph Harun al-Rashid's reign marked a peak in Baghdad's cultural and economic prosperity.
Rise of the Abbasids Abu al-Abbas led a revolt against the Umayyads, establishing the Abbasid dynasty.
Splendors of Baghdad Baghdad became a cultural hub under the Abbasids, attracting scholars and artists.
Muslim Culture in Spain The Umayyad survivor established a Muslim state in Spain, promoting arts and learning.
The Muslim Empire Declines By the 850s, the Abbasid control weakened, leading to fragmentation of the empire.
Seljuk Turks and Mongol Invasions The Seljuk Turks adopted Islam and built a large empire, threatening the Byzantine Empire.

Key Vocabulary: Abu Bakr- Muhammad’s father-in-law, 1st caliph Caliph- Successor of Muhammad, religious leader Sunni- Any religious Muslim from Muhammad’s tribe can lead the community Shiite-Believe that only Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali or his descendants can rule.

How did Muslims overcome early challenges to Islam?
Abu Bakr was selected to become the first ruler and successor to Muhammad.
After battles with wavering tribes, he reunited the Muslims based on their allegiance to Islam.

They began by converting the remaining Arab tribes to Islam, which ended the warfare between Arabs and united them under one leader.
Under the first four caliphs.
The Arabs surprised their neighbors and conquered great portions of the Byzantine empire and defeated the Persians entirely.
Describe differences between Sunni and Shiite Muslims.
The Shiites felt that Muhammad had designated his son-in-law, Ali to become his successor, and that the true successors are only descendants of Ali or Muhammad’s daughter, Fatisma.
These descendants, called Imams, are divinely inspired religious leaders, who are empowered to interpret the Quran and actions of Muhammad.
The Sunnis felt that any good Muslim could lead the community, since there are no prophets after Muhammad.
The majority of Muslims eventually became Sunnis and the successor was decided to be a pious male Muslim from Muhammad’s tribe, called a caliph, a political leader of the religious community.
What are three reasons for the success of Muslim conquests?
The weakness of the Byzantine & Persian empires provided it easy for Muslim to conquer.
People welcomed the Arabs as liberators from their harsh rule.
The Arab’s bold efficient fighting methods also lead its way to success.
(ex. War of Yarmuk). The Muslim also formed treaties and alliances with Spain to maintain powers.
Share cultures and traditions as well as standing in the same side against enemies.
How did Islam become a more universal faith?
As Muslim civilization developed, many Jews & Christians played key roles as officials, doctors and translators.
Muslim leaders wisely prohibited looting and destruction of conquered lands, ensuring continued wealth and prosperity for the empire in form of thrive and advantages.
However, many were drawn to Islam’s simple and direct messages for them to see its triumph as a sign of God’s favor.
Most nomadic in North Africa and Central Asia chose Islam immediately.
Islam have no religious hierarchy (class of priests).
It emphasizes the equality of all believers, regardless of race, gender, or wealth.

title: What caused the Abbasid dynasty to decline?
points: The Abbasids never ruled Spain and Starting about 850, their control over the rest of Muslim empire fragmented.
As Caliph’s powers faded in some regions, Shiite rulers came to power with a series of invasion.
In 1216, Genghis Kran led the Mongols out of the Central Asia across southwest Asia, returning again and again.
In 1258, Hulagu, the great grandson of Genghis, burned and looted Baghdad, killing the last Abbasid Caliph.
In the late 1300s, another Mongol leader, Timur the lame, or Tamerlane, led his armies to the Middle East.
His ambitions led him to conquered Muslim and non-Muslim lands, ending the Abbasid dynasty.

10.3 Muslim Civilization’s Golden Age Key Vocabulary: Social mobility- The ability to move up in social class Firdawsi- Poet who wrote in Persian using Arabic script Omar Khayyam- Famous scholar and astronomer, best known for the “The Rubaiyat” Calligraphy- The art of beautiful handwriting Ibn Rushd- The philosopher known in Europe as Averroes – put all knowledge except Quran in the text of reason Ibn Khaldum- An Arab thinker who set standards for scientific study of history Al-Khwarizmi- Muslim mathematician who pioneered the study of algebra Muhammad al-Razi- Medical thinker, head physician at Baghdad’s (books on medicine) chief hospital Ibn Sina- Famous Persian physician, canon on medicine (Encyclopedia for disease treatment) Q1.
What achievements did Muslims make in economics, art, literature, and science?
Between 750 and 1350, merchants built a vast trading network across Muslim lands and beyond.
Camel Caravans (ride on horseback) were called the “ships of the desert”.

Manufactured goods were highly valued.
Muslim artisans produced a wealth of fine goods.
Religion and belief shaped the arts and literature of Muslim.
Muslim art and literature reflected the diverse traditions of the various people living under Muslim’s rule, such as Greeks, Indians, Romans, and Persians.
Poets tell story such as “Ten Thousand and One Nights”.
Domes, Mosques, and High Minarets dominated the city, decorated with geometric patterns and calligraphy within.
Al-Khwarizmi is the Muslim mathematician who pioneered the study of algebra.
Muslim made remarkable advances in medicine and public health.
Muhammad al-Razi was a medical thinker and head physician at Baghdad’s chief hospital and wrote books on medicine.
Ibn Sina was a famous Persian physician, canon on medicine, and wrote an encyclopedia for disease treatment.
What business practices were pioneered by merchants in Muslim lands?
Extensive trade and a money economy led Muslims to pioneer new business practices.
They created partnerships, bought and sold on credit, formed banks in all major cities, so a check written in Baghdad might be cashed in Cairo.

title: What elements characterized Muslim art?
points: Muslim art reflected diverse traditions of the various people and distinctive style.
Artists were forbidden to use human or animal figures in religious art.
Quran is a very important source for Muslim literature such as poetry.
Most of the religious buildings were decorated with arabesque of abstract geometric patterns and calligraphy mosques had a dome and arches – Byzantine style.
Why did Islam prohibit the depiction of people or animals in religious art?
How did Muslim scholars preserve and build on the learning of earlier civilizations?
They achieved it by collecting classical works of ancient Greeks, Romans, Persians, and other early civilizations into libraries, translating them into Arabic and expanding the ideas within.
They also helped spread Arabic numerals which was invented by ancient Indians.

Athenians Win at Marathon 490 B.C. Persian army landed near Marathon.
Athenians used hand-to-hand combat to defeat the Persians.

City-States Unite In 480 B.C., Darius (the previous leader of Persians)’s son Xerxes sent a stronger force to conquer Greece, but Athens had already united with nearby city-states and thus grew a stronger force.

The first defensive army of Greece was made up of the Spartans, and they were defeated in the end. The Persians kept marching south and burnt the city of Athens (the people of Athens had already withdrawn to safe places).

Athenians used the fleet of boats which the king of Spartans had built to defeat the Persians. Athenians lured the Persian Navy into the narrow strait of Salamis and used the underwater battering rams to attack the enemy boats. As a result, the Persian Navy sank.
In 479 B.C., the Greeks defeated the Persians in Asia Minor.
Creation of the Delian League

Athens was the most powerful city-state during the war. Thus, Athenians organized an alliance (agreement) between two or more city-states to cooperate and come to one another’s defense. It was known as the Delian League.
Athens gained its position among the Delian League, and slowly created an Athenian Empire.

title: Two Golden Ages of China
points: The Tang Dynasty Reunifies China

After the Han dynasty collapsed in 220, China remained divided for nearly 400 years. During the brief period of the Sui dynasty (589-618), China was unified by the South and North, but the glory was not restored until the emergence of the Tang dynasty in 618.
The Tang Build an Empire The first emperor of the Tang dynasty, Li Yuan, was originally a general under the Sui dynasty. Sought the throne encouraged by his ambitious 16-year-old son, Li Shimin.
After Li Yuan ruled the Tang dynasty for 8 years, Li Shimin compelled his father to give up the throne, and having Li Shimin ruling the dynasty. Then, Li Shimin took the name Tang Taizong.
Li Shimin was a brilliant general, government reformer, historian and master of calligraphy.
Li Shimin expanded the territories into Central Asia and forced neighboring lands to become tributary states.
Spread culture to neighboring countries.
The Government and Economy Grow
Tang Rulers restored the Han bureaucracy & enlarged the civil system.
Allowed the government to recruit more talented people.
Trained in Confucian philosophy.
Develop schools to prepare for the exams.
Created a new law code. Instituted system of land reform.
Redistributed land held by local authorities/large agricultural holdings allow peasants to get a fraction of land.
Strengthened central power by weakening the landowners’ economic power.
Increased government revenue, more peasants pay tax.
The Tang Dynasty Declines The Tang dynasty eventually lost territories in Central Asia and to the Arabs.
In 907, a rebellion occurred and overthrew the Tang dynasty.
The Song Dynasty In 960, a scholarly general named Zhao Kuangyin ruled China and formed the Song dynasty.
Lasted for 319 years. Gained fewer territories than the Tang dynasty.
Faced constant threats from invaders from the north.
In the early 1100s, the Song dynasty retreated to the south of the Huang River.
Eventually, in the late 1200s, Song was overthrown by the Mongols.
Song dynasty developed the economy and culture.
People created new farming methods during the Song dynasty. Another type of rice was imported from Southeast Asia, which allowed people to harvest more crops.
The more crops allowed people to use it to sell for money, at the same time enhanced the economy and provide surplus resources to let people discover other matters, such as arts and commerce.
The Song dynasty constructed canals.
E.g. the Grand Canal, transported grain from south to northern China.
Foreign Trade flourished. Trade routes with India, Persia, Arabia, etc., had opened.
China’s Ordered Society The Gentry Value and Education
Gentry: Wealthy landowning class
Most scholar-officials came from the gentry. They studied Confucian classics for years to pass the civil service exam.
Gentry often served as allies of the emperor’s officials.
Gentry valued learning more than physical labor. Supported the revival of Confucian thoughts. Take Confucian officials as the ones that are wise and clever in the society.
Peasants Work the Land Many of the Chinese depended on crops to live their life, but some of them made small handicrafts and sold them to increase their earning.
People lived in small villages, where they depended on each other rather than believing in the government.
When arguments took place, a village leader and a council of elders would come to solve the problem.
Merchants Have Lowest Status
According to Confucian traditions, merchants had a lower social status than peasants since their wealth came from the labor of others.
Merchants needed to be educated to enter the gentry.
The Status of Women Women had a relatively high status in the Tang and early Song dynasties compared to later periods.
Women in families tended to run family affairs, such as managing servants and family finances.
A male’s status is still higher than a female’s. When women got married to men, they could not keep their dowry and could never remarry.
The tradition of Foot Binding emerged in the late Song dynasty. Acted as a symbol of nobility and beauty.
The Tang and Song Dynasties Develop a Rich Culture
Artists Paint Harmony Triumph in landscape painting during Song dynasty. Painters aimed to capture the spiritual essence of nature.
Architect and Porcelain. The Indian stupa evolved into the Chinese pagoda, a multistoried temple with eaves that curve up at the corners.
Created statues of Buddha.
Chinese Writing Libai, Dufu, etc. Y’all know this.

title: Korea and Its Traditions
points: Geography of the Korean Peninsula
Living among mountains and seas
Low but steep mountains Taebaek mountain range
Farming was difficult Most people lived along the western coastal plains
Thousands of islands Depended on seafood for protein in their diet
Location impacts Korea Received many cultural and technological influences from China
China extended political control over the Korean peninsula in history
The cultural bridge linking China and Japan
Adapted and transformed Chinese traditions, then passed them on to Japan
Evolved their own ways of living before the Chinese influence
Wudi invaded Korea and set up a military colony there
Confucian traditions Chinese governmental ideas
Chinese writing Farming methods
Development of the Silla and Koryo Dynasties
Three kingdoms: Koguro, Paekche, and Silla
Shared same language Shared same cultural background
Warred with one another or with China
Chinese cultures influenced them
Missionaries spread Buddhism
Korean monks travelled to China and India to learn more about Buddhism
Silla Kingdom united the Korean peninsula
Had only three dynasties Silla Dynasty united kingdoms
Became a tributary state under China
Preserved its independence
Confucian ideas affected the rights of women
Before Women had the right to inherit property
Upper-class women held public roles
After Can’t inherit properties
Subordinate family roles Modified Confucian ideas
Conflicts between peasants and the aristocrats led to the overthrow of the Silla dynasty
The Koryo dynasty Confucianism and Buddhism were both influential
Used woodblock printing for Buddhist texts
Improved Chinese inventions
Learned to make porcelain (celadon)
Celadon: porcelain with an unusual blue-green glaze
The Choson Dynasty Rules for Over 500 Years
Mongols invaded Korea and rule collapsed
Yi Song-gye set up the Choson dynasty
Longest dynasty among the three
Reduced Buddhist Confucian government
Korea creates alphabet King Sejong
Replace the Chinese writing system
Developed hangul Increased literacy rate
Japan invades 12.4 I. Geography Sets Japan Apart
Archipelago: Japan is a chain of islands (Hokkaido, Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku) located 100 miles off the Asian mainland. archipelago: A chain of islands.
Mountains: 4/5 of Japan is mountainous, limiting farmland.
Climate: Mild climate and sufficient rainfall support agriculture in narrow river valleys and coastal plains.
Seas: Protected Japan from invasion but also isolated it, allowing selective borrowing from
China and Korea. tsunami: Killer tidal waves caused by underwater earthquakes.
Ring of Fire: Japan is prone to volcanic activity and earthquakes.
II. Early Traditions Yamato Clan:
Dominated Japan by A.D. 500, claiming descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu.
Established Japan’s first and only dynasty.
Shinto:- Shinto: "The way of the kami," a religion honoring natural forces and spirits.
Shrines are located in natural settings like mountains, waterfalls, and ancient trees.
Korean artisans and metalworkers brought advanced skills.
Buddhism introduced to Japan in the 500s via Korea, along with Chinese writing and culture.
III. Japan Looks to China Prince Shotoku:
Sent nobles to study in China during the Tang Dynasty (600s-800s).
Adopted Chinese ideas on government, including the title "Heavenly Emperor" and a centralized bureaucracy.
Japan adopted and modified Chinese culture, rejecting the civil service exam but keeping
Confucian ethics. Developed kana: Phonetic symbols for writing Japanese. kana: Japanese phonetic symbols representing syllables.
Capital at Nara modeled after Chang’an (Tang China).
Nobles adopted Chinese fashion, food, and tea ceremonies.IV. The Heian Period (794-1185)
Capital moved to Heian (Kyoto).
Fujiwara Clan: Married daughters to emperors, gaining real power.
Elegant court life with strict etiquette and elaborate dress.
Sei Shonagon: Wrote The Pillow Book, detailing court life.
Murasaki Shikibu: Wrote The Tale of Genji, the world’s first novel. bushido: The samurai code of honor, emphasizing loyalty, bravery, and self-discipline.

The Tokugawas Unite Japan After the Mongol invasions, the Kamakura shogunate crumbled. New power took place in 1338, and warfare in 1450. Daimyo gave arms to peasants and samurai, causing chaotic conflicts.
By 1590, Toyotomi Hideyoshi had brought most of Japan together. Failed to conquer China and Korea.
In 1600, the daimyo Tokugawa Ieyasu became the master of Japan. Three years later, named shogun.
The Tokugawa Shogunate ruled Japan until 1868.
Central Government Imposed
The Tokugawa shoguns ended feudal warfare.
Maintained outward forms of feudal society but imposed central government control on all of Japan.
^ Called Centralized Feudalism.
Tokugawa needed to control the daimyo.
Daimyo needed to live in Edo (nowadays Tokyo) every other year. Daimyo’s family needed to be living in Edo full time.
Shoguns forbade Daimyo from repairing castles or marrying without permission.
New laws had strict social hierarchy. Only samurai were able to serve in the military or hold government jobs.
People in the lower class were forbidden to wear luxuries.
The Economy Booms New tools for agriculture emerged, allowing for more crop production. Hence, it supported population growth.
Trade flourished, and roads connecting cities were built.
Japanese merchants gained social status despite the influence of Confucian thoughts.
Zen Buddhism Shapes Culture
A Buddhist sect from China called Zen had been widely accepted by the samurai in Japan. It emphasized self-resilience, meditation, and devotion to duty.
Artistic Tradition Changed
In the 1300s, feudal culture had produced Noh plays performed on a square, wooden stage without scenery.
1600s, towns developed a drama called Kabuki.

title: A Time of Crisis The Black Death: A Global Epidemic
points: Autumn 1347: a fleet of Genoese trading ships loaded with grain left the Black Sea port of Caffa and set sail for Messina, Sicily.
Sailors started falling sick during the voyage.
Town people at Sicily became sick as well after the crew arrived.
Soon, the disease was called as Black Death from Italy. Soon reached Spain and France.
The Plague Spreads from Asia
Black Death: bubonic plague, a disease spread by fleas carried by rats.
Once emerged all around the world, but subsided. However, left a strain in Mongolia survived.
In 1200s, Mongols conquered Asia, probably set the background for the epidemic.
Normal Life Breaks Down The plague brought terror.
People turn to magic and witchcrafts for cure.
Wild pleasure Beat themselves with nailed whip. (flagellation)
Christians blamed Jews for the plague. Thousands of Jews were slaughtered.
The Economy Suffers Since workers and employees died, production declined.
Inflation broke out. Landowners converted cropland into land for sheep raising.
Peasants revolt during 1300s to 1400s, since they scarcely get jobs.
Upheaval in the Church The Church Splits
In 1309, Pope Clement V had moved the papal court to Avignon outside the border of southern France.
Pope had lavish court Criticism of this pleasure emerged.
Reformers worked for change
In 1378, Reformers elected their own Pope in Rome.
French church chose a rival pope as respond.
Schism occurred at this time.
New Heresies People dissatisfied with the church. People started to have new ideas, of following the Bible instead of the church.
The Hundred Years’ War A destructive war between France and England (1337 to 1453).
England and France both rival for control.
E.g. the English Channel. English Won Early Victories
New invention of weapon: Longbow utilized by English archers
Joan Arc Fought for France
17-year-old peasant woman, lead the French to multiple victories.
Taken by English allies captives, convicted and burned at the stake.
French saw her as a martyr.
1453, French gained victories using cannon.
Impact of the Hundred Years’ War
Created national feelings French king expand power.
English Parliament gained power, which they funded the ruler.

title: The Renaissance in Italy
points: A) What was the Renaissance?
Time of creativity Great change in
Political Social Economical
Cultural Shift from agricultural -> urban society
More trade Creative thinking
New technology A new worldview evolves
Reawakened interest in the classical learning of Greece and Rome
Used Latin for school and in church
Focused on religion and spirit
Explore the richness and variety of human experience
New emphasise on individual achievement
Ideal: a person with talents in many fields
A spirit of adventure Led people to explore new worlds
Reexamine old world Expressing humanism
Humanists studied the classical culture of Greece and Rome
Focused on worldly subjects rather than on the religious issues that had occupied medieval thinkers
Humanists believed education stimulates the individual’s creative powers
Humanities: subjects such as grammar, rhetoric, poetry, and history
B) Italy: Cradle of the Renaissance
Renaissance began in Italy
Italy’s History and Geography
Centre of the Roman Empire -> logical place for this reawakening to emerge
Architectural remains Statues
Coins Roman catholic church
Patron of the arts Inspiration for religious themes used by artists and writers
Location Encouraged trade with well-developed markets on the eastern Mediterranean, northern Africa, and northern Europe
Trade by ships Supported trading
Banking Manufacturing Marchant networks development
Trade provided the wealth that fueled Italy’s renaissance
Trade routes carried new ideas
Italy’s vibrant city-states
Divided into many small city-states
Each controlled by a powerful family
Dominated by a wealthy and powerful merchant class
Both political and economic leadership
Their emphasis on art and personal achievement helped to shape the Italian Renaissance
Medici family of Florence Ranked among the richest merchants and bankers in Europe
Cosimo de Medici gained control of the Florentine government
The family continued as uncrowned ruler of the city
Lorenzo Medici: “the Magnificent”
Represented the Renaissance ideal
Held Florence together during difficult times in the late 1400s
Financial supporter of the arts
Poets and philosophers frequently visited the Medici palace
Artists learned their craft by sketching the statues in the Medici garden
Symbolised energy and brilliance of the Italian Renaissance
C) Renaissance Art Flowers
Reflecting humanist thought
Reflected the ideas of humanism
Portrayed religious themes
Often set religious figures such as Jesus and Mary against classical Greek or Roman backgrounds
Painted famous portraits Revived classical forms
Using new artistic techniques
Used new techniques to represent landscapes and human
Rules of perspective helped to create realistic art
Made distant objects smaller than those close to the viewer, the scenes are more 3-dimensional
Sculptors and painters studied human anatomy
Architecture: a “social art”
To blend beauty with utility and improvement of society
Architects rejected the Gothic style of the late Middle Ages as disorderly
Adopted the columns, arches, and domes that had been favoured by the Greeks and Romans
Filippo Brunelleschi Created a majestic dome
Multi-talented Art Sculpture
Engineer Inventor Leonardo Da Vinci
Made sketches of nature and of models in his studio
Dissected corpses to learn about anatomy
His paintings griped humans with realism
Mona Lisa The Last Supper Religious painting
Masterpiece of perspective
Experimented with a new type of paint
Multi-talented Botany Anatomy
Optics Music Architecture Engineering
Sculptor Engineer Painter Architect
Dome of St. Peter’s Cathedral in Rome
Poet “Melancholy genius” His work reflects his many life-long spiritual and artistic struggles
David and the Pieta Captures the sorrow of the Biblical Mary as she cradles her dead son Jesus on her knees
Statue of David Biblical shepherd
Killed the giant Goliath Recalls the harmony and grace of ancient Greek tradition
Sistine Chapel in Rome One of his greatest projects
Depicted the biblical history of the world from the Creation to the Flood
Raphael “Sweet and gracious nature”
He developed his own style of painting that blended Christian and classical style
Tender portrayals of the Madonna, the mother of Jesus
The School of Athens Pictured an imaginary gathering of great thinkers and scientists
D) Writing for a New Society
Castiglione’s ideal courtier
Most famous: The Book of the Courier
Describes the manners, skills, learning, and virtues that a member of the court should have
His ideal courtier was a well-educated, well-mannered aristocrat who mastered many fields, from poetry to music to sport
His ideal differed for men and women
Man Athletic but not overactive
Good at games but not a gambler
Plays musical instruments and knows literature and history but is not arrogant
Women Offers a balance to men
Graceful and kind Lively and reserved
Beautiful on both inner and outer side
Machiavelli’s successful prince
Machiavelli wrote a guide for ruler on how to gain and maintain power
Didn’t discuss leadership in terms of high ideals
Book: The Prince Looked at real rulers in an age of ruthless power politics
The end justifies the means
Urged rulers to use whatever methods were necessary to achieve their goals
He saw himself as an enemy of oppression and corruption

title: The Renaissance in the North
points: The Printing Revolution In 1455, Johann Gutenberg of Mainz, Germany printed the first complete edition of Bible using movable printing method.
Printing revolution began At that time, only a few hundreds of books
By 1500, 15 to 20 millions of books were produced
Printed books are cheaper.
With more books available, more and more people started to read.
Exposed Europeans to new ideas and places.
Northern Renaissance Artists
Northern Renaissance began in the cities of Flanders. (active trading center)
Flemish Painters 1400s, Jan van Eyck portrayed town people and religious scenes with rich realistic details.
1500s, Pieter Bruegel portrayed peasant life using vibrant colors. “Peasant Bruegel”
1600s, Peter Paul Rubens blended classical realistic paintings and the artistic freedom of the Italian Renaissance.
Rubens had a wide knowledge of mythology, the Bible, and classical history.
Dürer: “Leonardo of the North”
1494, German painter Albrecht Dürer traveled to Italy to study with the Italian masters.
Pioneering of spreading Renaissance idea in northern Europe.
Transferreed the skill of painting into engraving to make prints
Portrayed religious upheaval.
Northern Humanists and Writers
Humanist scholars use Latin and vernacular, or everyday language to write
Eramus: Making Humanism Popular
The Dutch priest and humanist Desiderius Erasmus created Greek edition of Bible.
Spread Renaissanc humanism
Called for the translation of Bible into the vernacular.
Called for reforms in church
Sir Thomas More’s Ideal Society
Pressed for social reforms
Wrote Utopia, portrayed an ideal world.
Rabelais’ Comic Masterpiece
François Rabelais wrote Gargantua and Pantagruel, adventure of two giants.
Having doubts about Catholic churches.
Shakespeare Writes for All Time
English poet and playwright.
Between 1590 and 1613, he wrote 37 plays.
Explores Renaissance ideals. Such as complexity of individuals and importance of classics

title: The Search for Spices
points: Motivation for Exploring the Seas
Europeans traded with Asians long time ago.
The Crusades introduced luxury goods to Europe from Asia.
Most valued item during their trade was the spices.
Chief source of spices was Moluccas.
Most goods from Asia were brought to Europe by Italian traders. They carried the goods from East Mediterranean which had goods previously dropped by the Muslim traders.
Other Europeans realized that having direct access to Asia would reduce a large amount of cost which they had previously spent on the Italian traders.
Portugal Sails East Prince Henry sponsored the Portugal explorations.
Mapping the African Coast Prince Henry seized the chance of converting African, who originally believed in Islam or tribal religions, to Christians.
Prince Henry also wanted to reach Asia in an easier way, with going around the Southern tip of Africa.
Cartographers – map makers
Seeking India In 1497, Vasco da Gama led the troupes around the Southern tip of Africa (Cape of Good Hope)
Da Gama eventually reached port of Calicut, on the west coast of India.
Da Gama made large profit out of the spices, and dominated main ports on the coast of India.
Columbus Sails West Italian navigator named Christopher Columbus wanted to reach East India, so he voyaged from Europe to the West.
Reaching Faraway Lands Columbus persuaded Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain to sponsor him.
On August 3, 1492, Columbus set sail to the west in three small ships.
On October 12, a land came in sight.
He assumed that he encountered the Indies, so he called the people Indians.
Dividing the Globe in Half

In 1493 Pope Alexander VI set a Line of Demarcation, dividing the non-European world into two zones. Spain has the right to trade and explore on the west side, while Portugal has the right to trade and explore on the east side.
The terms of the Line were agreed to in the Treaty of Tordesillas, signed between two countries in 1494.
Naming the Western Hemisphere
In 1507, a German cartographer named the Brazil region as “America”.
The islands Columbus had explored in the Caribbean had been known as the West Indies.
The Search for a Direct Route Continues
On September 20, 1519, a Portuguese nobleman named Ferdinand Magellan set out for finding a way to the Pacific with five ships. At last, he reached the coast of South America.
In November 1520, Magellan and his crew entered a bay, and found a strait leading to the Pacific, would later be known as the Magellan Strait.
They sailed for nearly four months, then reached the Philippines, where Magellan was killed.

After setting out from Portugal for three years, the remaining survivors came back to Spain. Magellan’s expedition is considered the first to circumnavigate the Earth, even though Magellan himself did not survive the journey.

title: Civilizations of Mesoamerica
points: A) People Settle in the Americas
Migration to the Americas Occurred between 60,000 and 18,000 B.C., likely from Asia.
Took place during the last Ice Age when sea levels dropped.
A land bridge (now the Bering Strait) connected Siberia and Alaska.
Migration possibly occurred along coastal routes via small boats, not just the land bridge.
Adaptation to Environments
Settlers spread through diverse regions—icy lands in the north, rainforests near the equator, and deserts in the south.
Adapted by developing hunting skills and domesticating plants and animals.
Agricultural Developments Between 8500 B.C. and 2000 B.C., people began farming.
Crops in Mesoamerica included maize (corn), beans, squash, peppers, tomatoes, and sweet potatoes.
In South America, crops included maize and cassava; llamas were domesticated for wool and labour.
Village and City Formation
By 3000 B.C. in South America and 1500 B.C. in Mesoamerica, settled farming villages emerged.
These villages eventually grew into the first cities of the Americas.
B) Civilisation Arises with the Olmecs
Location and Timeframe Emerged along the Gulf Coast of Mexico in tropical forests.
Flourished from about 1200 B.C. to 400 B.C.
Social Structure Dominated by a powerful class of priests and nobles.
The elite lived in ceremonial centres; common people lived in surrounding villages.
Art and Architecture Known for colossal stone heads (up to 40 tons), likely representing rulers.
Also created jade figurines and other stone artworks.
Built ceremonial centres without wheeled vehicles or draft animals.
Invented a calendar system.
Developed hieroglyphic writing carved into stone.
Trade and Cultural Influence
Engaged in wide-ranging trade.
Cultural motifs such as jaguars and serpents influenced later Mesoamerican societies.
Regarded as the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica for their foundational contributions.

title: Andean Civilisations A) Cultures Develop in the Andes
points: Geographic Setting Andean region includes coastal deserts, high mountain plateaus, and jungles east of the Andes.
Harsh climate and geography required significant adaptation.
Early Settlements and Agriculture
Coastal fishing villages in Peru and Chile were the first settlements.
Inland farming developed in river valleys and plateaus.
Crops included maize, cotton, squash, and beans; over 700 types of potatoes were cultivated.
Llamas and alpacas were domesticated for labour, meat, and wool.
Cultural Achievements Built ceremonial centres.
Developed pottery, weaving, and irrigation techniques.
B) Notable Andean Cultures
Chavín (c. 900–200 B.C.) Located at Chavín de Huantar in northern and central Peru.
Built a massive temple complex.
Religion likely unified various regions and influenced later Andean societies.
Moche (A.D. 100–700) Based along the northern coast of Peru.
Constructed the largest adobe (sun-dried clay) structure in the ancient Americas.
Farming (fertilised soil and used irrigation canals).
Engineering (built roads and relay runner networks).
Art (created lifelike ceramic vessels, goldwork, textiles, and wood carvings).
Nazca (c. 200 B.C.–A.D. 500)
Located on the southern coast of Peru.
Created geoglyphs—massive desert drawings of lines and animals like birds and whales.
Believed to have spiritual or religious significance.
Huari and Tiahuanaco (A.D. 650–750)
Huari: Controlled the mountain and coastal regions of Peru.
Tiahuanaco: Located near Lake Titicaca in modern-day Bolivia.
Influenced areas of modern Argentina, Chile, and Peru.
Shared similar art styles, suggesting:
Religious connections. Possible trade alliances or shared cultural foundations.

title: CONQUEST IN THE AMERICAS
points: A) First Encounters in the Americas
Meeting the Taínos
Columbus encountered the Taíno people when he first arrived in the West Indies
Taínos were open and friendly toward the Spanish
Taínos were “generous with what they have, to such a degree as no one would believe but he who had seen it.”
Taínos offended the Spanish when they failed to respect the Christian symbol properly
Columbus felt that he was superior to the Taínos and could decide their fate
Columbus claimed the land for Spain
Columbus took several Taínos as prisoners to take back to the Spanish king
Columbus’s encounter was repeated by a wave of Spanish conquistadors who soon arrived in the Americas
Conquistadors: conquerors They first settled on the lands of Hispaniola, Cuba, and Puerto Rico
They seized the Native Americans’ gold ornaments
Made them pan for more gold IDX G9 HISTORY S+ STUDY GUIDE ISSUE S2
FINALS Forced the Native Americans to convert to Christianity
Guns, Horses, and Disease
Spanish guns and cannons were superior to the Native Americans’ arrows and spears
European metal armour provided the Spanish with better protection
The Spanish had horses Useful in battles
Carrying supplies Frightened the Native Americans because they had never seen a horse
Disease helped the conquistadors take control of the Taínos and other Native
Americans Europeans carried diseases that Native Americans had no immunity to
Smallpox Measles Influenza
The diseases spread rapidly and wiped out villages
The Native American population declined by 90% in the 1500s
B) Corté s Conquers Mexico
Cortés advances on the Aztecs
Hernán Cortés One of the earliest conquistadors
A landowner in Cuba Heard of Spanish expeditions that had been repelled by Indians
Believed that he could succeed where none had before
1519, landed on the coast of Mexico
Began an inland trek toward Tenochtitlán
Tenochtitlán: the capital of the Aztec empire
Young Indian women
Served as Cortés’s translator and advisor
Knew both the Maya and Aztec languages
Learned Spanish quickly
Told Cortés that the Aztecs had gained power by conquering other groups of people
The Aztecs sacrificed thousands of their captives to the
Aztec gods each year Conquered people hated their Aztec overlords
Malinche helped Cortés arrange alliances with them
Conquered people agreed to help Cortés fight the Aztecs
Moctezuma faces a dilemma
Moctezuma Aztec emperor Wondered if the leader was Quetzalcoatl
Quetzalcoatl: an Aztec god -king who had long ago vowed to return from the east
Did not know how to respond to the arrival of Cortés because he wasn’t sure if Cortés was a god
Sent gifts with religious importance
Urged the strangers not to continue to Tenochtitlán
Cortés was not interested in Aztec religious objects, but was extremely interested in the gold and silver ornaments that Moctezuma sent him
Cortés became more determined than ever to reach Tenochtitlán
Tenochtitlan falls to the Spanish
The Spanish scorned the Aztecs’ religion and sought to convert them to Christianity
The Spanish saw more of the Aztec treasure in Tenochtitlan, so they decided to imprison Motezuma so they could gain control of the Aztecs and their riches
Cortés compelled Moctezuma to sign over his land and treasure to the Spanish
A new force of Spanish conquistadors had arrived on the coast to challenge Cortés
Various groups of Spanish, Aztecs, and Native Americans all fought for control
The Aztecs drove the Spanish from the city
More than half of the Spanish were killed in the fighting
Moctezuma was killed in the fighting
Cortés retreated to plan an assault
Cortés captured and demolished Tenochtitlán
The Spanish later built Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlán
C) Pizarro Takes Peru Cortés’s success inspired other adventurers
Interested in Peru’s Inca empire, which was reputed to have even more riches than the Aztecs
Arrived in Peru just after the Incan ruler Atahualpa had won the throne from his brother in a bloody civil war
Atahualpa refused to become a Spanish vassal or convert to Christianity
Pizarro captured Atahualpa and slaughtered thousands of Incas with the aid of Indian allies
The Spanish demanded a huge ransom for the ruler
The Inca paid it
Atahualpa was still killed by the Spanish
Pizarro and his followers overran the Incan heartland
He had superior weapons
The Incas were weakened by European diseases
Spanish forces surged across Ecuador and Chile
Pizarro was killed by a rival Spanish faction a few years after he established the city of Lima
D) Effects of the Spanish Conquistadors
The Spanish Victory
A few hundred European soldiers had conquered millions of Native Americans
Seized huge quantities of valuable goods
Ha used Native American labour to establish silver mines in Peru and Mexico to finance their new empire
Treasure fleets sailed each year to Spain from the Spanish Philippines, loaded with gold and silver
Spain became Europe’s greatest power
Effects on Native Americans
Believed that the disasters they suffered marked the world’s end
Survivors from diseases felt that their gods were less powerful than the god of their conquerors
Many Native Americans converted to Christianity in the hopes that their suffering would end
Effects on Indians
Continued to resist the Spanish in any way they could
The Maya fought Spanish rule in Mexico and Central America
Revolts erupted among the Inca
Indians resisted European influences by preserving aspects of their own culture
Native American culture came to influence the culture of Latin America

title: SPANISH AND PORTUGUESE COLONIES IN THE AMERICAS
points: A) Ruling the Spanish Empire
Spain claimed a vast empire stretching from California to South America
Spain divided these lands into four provinces, including New Spain and Peru
Governing the provinces
Spain was determined to maintain strict control over its empire
The king set up the Council of the Indies
To pass laws for the colonies
Closely monitored the colonial officials to make sure they did not assume too much authority
Appointed viceroys Viceroys: representatives who rule in his name in each province
Lesser officials and audiencias helped the viceroy rule
Audiencias: advisory councils of Spanish settlers
To Spain, winning souls for Christianity was as important as gaining land
The Catholic Church worked with the government to convert Native Americans to
Church leaders often served as royal officials and helped to regulate the activities of
As Spain’s American empire expanded, Church authority expanded along with it
Missionaries Baptised thousands of Native Americans
Built mission churches Worked to turn new converts into loyal subjects of the Catholic king of Spain
Introduces European clothing
Introduced the Spanish language
Introduces new crafts such as carpentry and locksmithing
Forcibly imposed European culture over Native American culture
To make the empire profitable
The most valuable resources shipped from Spanish America to Spain were silver and gold
Colonists could export raw materials only to Spain and could buy only Spanish manufactured goods
Laws forbade colonists from trading with other European nations or even it other
Sugarcane became profitable
Had to be grown on plantations
Large estates run by an owner or the owner’s overseer
Plantation needed large numbers of workers to be profitable
Encomienda – A System of Forced Labour
Spanish monarchs granted the conquistadors encomiendas
Encomiendas: the right to demand labour to tribute from Native Americans in a particular area
The conquistadors used this system to force Native Americans to work under the most brutal conditions
Those who resisted were hunted down and killed
Disease, starvation, and cruel treatment caused drastic declines in the Native
Used in the mines as well as on plantations
Tons of silver from the Potisí region of Peru and Bolivia filled Spanish treasure ships
Native Americans were forced to extract the rich ore from dangerous shafts deep inside the Andes Mountains
Thousands of Indians die from the terrible conditions
A Spanish Priest Speaks Out
Bartolomé de Las Casas Condemned the evils of the encomienda system
Las Casas detailed the horrors that Spanish rule had brought to Native
Americans Pleaded with the king to end the abuse
Spain passed the New Laws of the Indies in 1542
The Laws forbade enslavement and abuse of Native Americans
Many Native Americans were forced to become peons
Peons: workers forced to labour for a landlord in order to pay off a debt
Landlords advanced workers with food, tools, or seed, creating debts that workers could never pay off in their lifetime
Bringing Workers From Africa
Las Casas urged colonists to import workers from Africa
He believed that Africans were immune to tropical diseases and had skills in farming, mining, and metalworking
Furthered the brutal African slave trade
The demand for sugar products skyrocketed
Millions of Africans were imported
Forced to work as field hands, miners, or servants
Became artists, artisans, and mechanics
Some Africans earned enough money to buy their freedom
Some rebelled or ran away B) Colonial Society and Culture
Settlers learned Native American styles of building
Ate American food Travelled in Indian -style canoes
Indian artistic styles influenced the newcomers
Europeans Taught their religion to Native Americans
Introduced animals -> transformed the lives of many Native Americans
Africans Introduced their farming methods
Cooking styles Crops Drama
Dance Songs A Layered Society
Peninsulares At the top of the social classes
Peninsulares: people born in Spain
Peninsular referred to the Iberian Peninsula
Filled the highest positions in both colonial governments and the Catholic
Creoles Creoles: American -born descendants of Spanish settlers
Owned most of the plantations, ranches, and mines
Mestizos Mestizos: people of Native American and European descent
Mulattoes Mulattoes: people of African and European descent
American and African descendants were in the lowest social classes
Lively Towns and Cities
Spanish settlers generally live in towns and cities
The population of Mexico City grew so quickly that it became the largest Spanish speaking city by the 1550s
Colonial cities Centres of government, commerce, and European culture
Around the central plaza stood government buildings and a Spanish -style church
Broad avenues and public monuments symbolised European power and wealth
Cities were also centres of intellectual and cultural life
Architecture, paintings, poetry, and the exchange of ideas flourished in Spanish cities in the Americas
Colonies built universities

title: Effects of Global Contact
points: I. The Columbian Exchange 1. After Christopher Columbus first discovered the Americas, he initiated trade between
Western Europe, also known as the Old World, and the Americas, also known as the
New World. This exchange process was later called the Columbian Exchange.
B. New Foods and Animals 1. The American foods tomatoes and corn satisfied the needs on food in the highly populated Europe. Soon it spreads even further, becomes an important crop worldwide.
2. European also carried crops to the Americas. For example, Europe brought grape and wheat, Africa and Asia had banana and sugar cane.
3. Cattles, pigs, goats, and chickens were brought to the Americas. Animals improve local Americans with a better diet, while the horses and donkeys allowed the
Americans to transport and hunt easily.
C. The Global Population Explodes
1. The American crops allowed the European population to increase by the 1700s.
2. The Columbian Exchange also allowed millions of people to migrate from Europe to the Americas through boats.
3. Atlantic slave trade forcibly brought millions of Africans to the Americas.
4. For the Native American population, it decreased, since they had no immunity toward
European diseases, for example, smallpox and measles.
II. A Commercial Revolution
A. The Price Revolution Strikes
1. During the 1500s, prices in European market started to rise. Too much money were in circulation, caused severe inflation.
2. The inflation was triggered by the enormous amount of silver and gold flowing into
Europe from the Americas by the mid -1500s.
3. This period is known as the price revolution.
B. Capitalism Emerges 1. Expanded trades allowed the growth of European capitalism.
2. Entrepreneurs are critical to the success of capitalism.
C. Exploring New Business Methods
1. Banks increased in importance, allowing wealthy merchants to lend money at interest.
D. Bypassing the Guilds 1. Capitalists bypassed the guilds using “putting -out” system. It was first used to produce textiles but later spread to other industries.
2. This system separated capital and labor for the first time, and it divides the work from raw material to the final product into different phases and different factories.

III. Mercantilism Arises 1. Mercantilism: Strengthen national economies. Believe that a nation’s real wealth was measured in its gold and silver treasure. A nation must export more goods than it imported.

B. The Role of Colonies 1. Mercantilism aimed to gain benefits from the colonies, thus, European powers passed strict laws regulating trade with their colonies. Colonists could not set up their own industries to manufacture goods.
C. Increasing National Wealth
1. Tariffs: Taxes on imported goods, designed to protect local industries from foreign competition by increasing the price of imported goods.

title: The Protestant Reformation
points: I. Background to the Reformation
1. In renaissance Italy, wealth was not distributed equally.
B. Church Abuses 1. Popes competed with Italian Princes for political power.
2. Protected Papal states from threatens of the secular states.
3. Church fought for power in their own interests.

4. Clergies sold indulgences to finance the artwork for the churches. a. Indulgence was a lessening of the time a soul would have to spend in purgatory, a place where souls too impure to enter heaven atoned for sins committed during their lifetimes.
5. Such practice stressed Bible study.
C. Early Revolts Against the Church
1. In England in the 1300s, John Wycliffe launched a systematic attack against the
Church, called for a change.
2. Jan Hus, born 40 years after Wycliffe, led a reform movement for which he was executed.
II. Martin Luther: Catalyst of Change
1. In 1517, protests erupted into a full -scale revolt. It was triggered by a German monk and professor of theology named Martin Luther.
B. Writing the 95 Theses 1. In 1517, Johann Tetzel collected indulgences, which outraged Luther. Luther soon drew 95 theses against indulgences.
C. Igniting a Firestorm 1. Overnight, copies of 95 theses were printed and distributed across Europe, and stirred furious debate.
2. Luther fought against the church and developed new doctrines.
3. In 1521, Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther.
4. The new Holy Roman emperor Charles V, summoned Luther to the diet at the city of
Worms. 5. Emperor ordered Luther to give up his protest. He again refused.
6. Emperor declared Luther an outlaw, making it a crime for anyone to give him food or shelter.
7. Still, Luther had a large amount of followers that support his arguments.
