3. Cattles, pigs, goats, and chickens were brought to the Americas.
Animals improve local Americans with a better diet, while the horses and donkeys allowed the Americans to transport and hunt easily.
C. The Global Population Explodes 1.
The American crops allowed the European population to increase by the 1700s.
The Columbian Exchange also allowed millions of people to migrate from Europe to the Americas through boats.
Atlantic slave trade forcibly brought millions of Africans to the Americas.
4. For the Native American population, it decreased, since they had no immunity toward European diseases, for example, smallpox and measles.
II. A Commercial Revolution A.
The Price Revolution Strikes 1.
During the 1500s, prices in European market started to rise.
Too much money were in circulation, caused severe inflation.
The inflation was triggered by the enormous amount of silver and gold flowing into Europe from the Americas by the mid -1500s.
This period is known as the price revolution.
Capitalism Emerges 1. Expanded trades allowed the growth of European capitalism.
Entrepreneurs are critical to the success of capitalism.
Exploring New Business Methods 1.
Banks increased in importance, allowing wealthy merchants to lend money at interest.
D. Bypassing the Guilds 1.
Capitalists bypassed the guilds using “putting -out” system.
It was first used to produce textiles but later spread to other industries.
This system separated capital and labor for the first time, and it divides the work from raw material to the final product into different phases and different factories.
III. Mercantilism Arises 1.
Mercantilism: Strengthen national economies.
Believe that a nation’s real wealth was measured in its gold and silver treasure.
A nation must export more goods than it imported.
The Role of Colonies 1. Mercantilism aimed to gain benefits from the colonies, thus, European powers passed strict laws regulating trade with their colonies.
Colonists could not set up their own industries to manufacture goods.
Increasing National Wealth 1.
Tariffs: Taxes on imported goods, designed to protect local industries from foreign competition by increasing the price of imported goods.

title: The Protestant Reformation I.
points: Background to the Reformation 1.
In renaissance Italy, wealth was not distributed equally.
Church Abuses 1. Popes competed with Italian Princes for political power.
Protected Papal states from threatens of the secular states.
Church fought for power in their own interests.
Clergies sold indulgences to finance the artwork for the churches. a.
Indulgence was a lessening of the time a soul would have to spend in purgatory, a place where souls too impure to enter heaven atoned for sins committed during their lifetimes.
5. Such practice stressed Bible study.
Early Revolts Against the Church 1.
In England in the 1300s, John Wycliffe launched a systematic attack against the Church, called for a change.
Jan Hus, born 40 years after Wycliffe, led a reform movement for which he was executed.
Martin Luther: Catalyst of Change 1.
In 1517, protests erupted into a full -scale revolt.
It was triggered by a German monk and professor of theology named Martin Luther.
Writing the 95 Theses 1. In 1517, Johann Tetzel collected indulgences, which outraged Luther.
Luther soon drew 95 theses against indulgences.
Igniting a Firestorm 1. Overnight, copies of 95 theses were printed and distributed across Europe, and stirred furious debate.
Luther fought against the church and developed new doctrines.
In 1521, Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther.
The new Holy Roman emperor Charles V, summoned Luther to the diet at the city of Worms.
Emperor ordered Luther to give up his protest.
He again refused. 6. Emperor declared Luther an outlaw, making it a crime for anyone to give him food or shelter.
7. Still, Luther had a large amount of followers that support his arguments.

title: Points and Lines Coordinate Geonetry
points: One-to-one correspondence between the set of real numbers and the set of points on the number line. Extending this concept, there is one-to-one correspondence between the set of points on the plane and the set of ordered pairs of real numbers.

One reference system used to represent this correspondence is called a rectangular, or Cartesian, coordinate system. x-axis – one horizontal number line y-axis – one vertical number line perpendicular to x-axis.
Origin – The point of intersection at the zero value on each line.
Coordinate axes – x- and y axes together
Quadrants – four parts that are formed by dividing the coordinate plane with the coordinate axes.
Each point P in the xy-plane can be assigned a unique ordered pair (x, y).

Linear Equations Given a set S of ordered pairs of numbers, each element of the set can be represented by a point in the plane. The graph of S is the set of all such points. x-intercept – The x-coordinate of the point where the graph of an equation intersects the x-axis. y-intercept – The y-coordinate of the point where the graph of an equation intersects the y-axis
Linear equation Ax+By=C, A B are not both zero: its graph is a line.

title: 5.Concurrent Lines, Medians, and Altitudes
points: When three or more lines intersect in one point, they are concurrent.
The point at. which they intersect is the point of concurrency.
For any triangle, four different sets of lines are concurrent.
The point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle is called the circumcenter of the triangle. ;:;,.>t-.!I;""'#>~>3!~""'"
'"< --- -The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle is called the incenter of the triangle.
A median of a triangle is a segment whose endpoints are a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

An altitude of a triangle is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. Unlike angle bisectors and medians, an altitude of a triangle can be a side of a triangle or it may lie outside the triangle.
The lines containing the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent at the orthocenter of the triangle.
Theorem 5-6: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices.
Theorem 5-8: The medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is two thirds the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Theorem 5-9: The lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

The point where a circle and a tangent intersect is the point of tangency

title: Concepts and Properties of Polygons
points: Polygon: closed, planar figure with ≥ 3 straight sides such that no three adjacent points are collinear and edges only intersect at common vertices.
Diagonal: a segment that connects two non-adjacent points in a polygon
Equilateral: All sides are congruent in length
Equiangular: All angles are congruent
Regular: Both Equilateral and Equiangular
Convex polygons: polygons which have all diagonals inside
Concave polygons: polygons that are not convex
How to determine whether a polygon is convex: check if any angle > 180; if so, it is concave; otherwise, it is convex.
All polygons are assumed to be convex in problems unless otherwise stated.
3.2 Parallelograms Parallelogram: Quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel (and equal)
Definition and formulas: see back
How to quickly construct an arbitrary parallelogram:
Draw a line k. Draw another line segment m, intersecting line k at A and of some length n.
Copy angle A on somewhere else on k.
Copy the length n. Connect the endpoints.

title: Special Parallelograms
points: 1. Rectangle: A parallelogram with 90 angles
2. Rhombus: A parallelogram with equal-length sides
3. Square: A parallelogram with 90 angles and equal-length sides
A rectangle has congruent diagonals.
A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals (so its area formula is 1/2 * d1 * d2, where d1and d2 are the lengths of its diagonals)
A square has congruent, perpendicular diagonals whose lengths are equal to * s, where s is the square's side length.
3.4 Trapezoids A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides (called bases); the non-parallel sides are its legs.
Area formula: (a + b) * h/2, where a and b are the lengths of the bases, and h is the height of the trapezoid (the distance between the bases).
Solving trapezoid problems:
Cut into a right triangle and a right trapezoid if it is isosceles.
Cut into a triangle and a parallelogram.
Cut along altitudes from the upper base to the lower base to get two RTs and a rectangle.
Construct parallel lines to the legs (basically 2).
Extend the legs to intersect at a point (very useful for isosceles trapezoids)
Right trapezoid: A trapezoid with a right angle.
Isosceles trapezoid: A trapezoid with congruent leg lengths.
Midsegment: a segment connecting the midpoint of the two legs.

points: There are different notations for sets:
They are written as: {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19}
Two sets are equal if they contain the same elements
A subset is if every element of Set A is also an element of Set B.
A proper subset is when a subset doesn’t include the fact that A = B.
An empty set is just: { }. A set that contains NO elements.
Sets are finite sets if n(A) has a definite value. Where if it has an endless amount, then it’s an infinite set.
The intersection of two sets A & B is the elements that are BOTH in A and B.
Union The union of two sets A & B is basically counting all the elements in both sets.
3) Complement of a Set:
A universal set (U) is the set of all elements.
The complement of a set is the universal set excluding the set that it’s a complement of.

points: The negation of a statement has the opposite truth value.

title: 1-New Term Isometric Drawing
points: An isometric drawing is a 2D representation of a 3D object where all three dimensions
(length, width, and height) are drawn at the same scale and at 30 -degree angles from the horizontal.
Key features for drawing:
30° Angles – Horizontal edges are drawn at 30° from the baseline (vertical lines remain straight).
Equal Scaling – All three axes (X, Y, Z) use the same scale (no foreshortening).
No Perspective – Parallel lines do not converge (unlike perspective drawings).
3D Representation – Shows width, height, and depth in a single view.
No Hidden Lines – Normally, only visible edges are shown (unless necessary for clarity).

title: E.g. ↓’s Isometric Drawing → → →
points: Orthographic Drawing An orthographic drawing is a 2D technical representation of a 3D object, showing multiple flat views (e.g., front, top, side) at right angles to each other.
Key features for drawing: Multiple 2D Views – Shows front, top, and right views (sometimes more).
90° Alignment – Views are perfectly aligned (top view directly above front view, side view to the side).
True Dimensions – Each view is drawn to scale without distortion.
Hidden Lines – Uses dashed lines to show obscured edges.
No Depth Illusion – Pure 2D representation (unlike isometric or perspective).
Front view ↓ Right view ↓ Top view ↓
Foundation Drawing Foundation Drawing is a 2D technical representation of a 3D object, usually showing the top view of it.
Each small figures have a number on it, represent its height.
Key Features for drawing: Top 2D View-Just show the top view, but also show the direction of it.
90° Alignment – Views are perfectly aligned (directly above front view ).
Entire arrangement-The figure should be divided into several regular cubes with edge 1 unit.
Counting necessity-Each small cubes should have a number of it to represent its height (how many cubes are used to stack it).
↓’s Foundation Drawing → → →
Net A net is a 2D pattern that can be folded along its edges to form a 3D geometric solid (e.g., cube, pyramid, prism).
Key Features for drawing: Complete Face Representation-Includes every face of the 3D shape (no missing or overlapping parts).
Edge Alignment-Edges that will join in 3D must match in length and position in the 2D net.
No Gaps or Overlaps-faces must connect edge -to-edge without extra space or unintended overlaps.
Foldable Design-Must be physically possible to fold into the intended 3D shape (e.g., valid cube nets have 11 distinct configurations).
Scale Accuracy-All faces must be proportionally sized to match the 3D solid.

points: 2.5 P roving Angles Congurent-Th 2-1 Vertical Angles Theorem: Vertical angles are congurent.
Th 2-2 Congurent Supplements Theorem: If 2 angles are supplements (180 degree) of the same angle (or of congruent angles), then the 2 angles are congruent.
Th 2-4 All right triangles are congruent-Th 2-5 If 2 angles are congruent and supplementary, then each is a right angle.
Chapter 3 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
3.1 P roperties of Parallel Lines-Postulate 3-1 Corresponding Angles Postulate: If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then corresponding angles are congruent.
Th 3-1 Alternate Interior Angles Theorem: If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then alternate interior angles are congruent.
Th 3-4 Same-Side Exterior Angles Theorem: If a transversal intersects 2 parallel lines, then same-side exterior angles are supplementary.
3.2 Proving lines parallel-Postulate 3-2 Converse of Corresponding Angles Postulate: If 2 lines and a transversal form corresponding angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel.
Th 3-5 Converse of Alternate Interior Angles Theorem: If 2 lines and a transversal form alternate interior angles that are congruent, then the 2 lines are parallel.
3.3 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines-Th 3-9: If 2 lines are parallel to the same line, then they are parallel to each other.
Th 3-10: In a plane, if 2 lines are perpendicular to the same line, then they are parallel to each other.
Th 3-11: In a plane, if a line is perpendicular to 1 of 2 parallel lines, the it is alos perpendicular to each other.
3.4 Parallel Lines and the Triangle Angle Sum Theorem-Th 3-12 Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem: The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is 180.
Th 3-13 Triangle Exterior Angle Theorem: The measure of each exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the measures of its 2 remote interior angles.
An exterior angle is an angle formed by a side and an extension of an adjacent side.
For each exterior angle of a triangle, the 2 nonadjacent interiors angles are its remote interior angles.

Classify a triangle by angles: - Equiangular: all angles congruent-Acute: all angles acute-Right: one right angle-Obtuse: one obtuse angle-Classify a triangle by sides: - Equilateral: all sides congruent-Isosceles: at least 2 sides congruent-Scalene: no sides congruent-Steps to classify triangle: Valid triangle: sum of 2 shortest sides should be greater than the remaining side (longest side) 2) Acute triangle: a² + b² > c² Right triangle: a² + b² = c² Obtuse triangle: a² + b²
< c² Chapter 4 Congruent Triangles
4.1 C ongruent Figures-Th 4-1: If 2 angles of one triangle are congruent to 2 sides of another triangle, then the 3rd angles are congruent.
4.2 Triangle Congruence by SSS and SAS-Postulate 4-1: (SSS) If the 3 sides of a triangle are congruent to the sides of another triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent.
Postulate 4-2: (SAS) If 2 pairs of sides are congruent and the included angles are also congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

Has to be included angle of 2 sides, no “SSA” 4.3 Triangle Congruence by ASA and AAS-Postulate 4-3: (ASA) If the 2 pairs of angles are congruent and the included sides are congruent, then the 2 triangles are congruent.
Th 4-2: (AAS) If 2 pairs of angles are congruent and a nonincluded side congruent to the correspnding nonincluded side of the other triangle, then the 2 triangles are congruent.

4.4 Using Congruent Triangles: CPCTC-CPCTC: (Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent) If 2 triangles are proven congruent by 3 congruences, then the other 3 congruences hold true too.

Isometric Drawing An isometric drawing is a 2D representation of a 3D object where all three dimensions (length, width, and height) are drawn at the same scale and at 30 -degree angles from the horizontal.
Key features for drawing: 30° Angles – Horizontal edges are drawn at 30° from the baseline (vertical lines remain straight).
Equal Scaling – All three axes (X, Y, Z) use the same scale (no foreshortening).
No Perspective – Parallel lines do not converge (unlike perspective drawings).
3D Representation – Shows width, height, and depth in a single view.
No Hidden Lines – Normally, only visible edges are shown (unless necessary for clarity).

title: Classical (1750–1820) Key word: enlightenment
points: Context: Enlightenment ideals—balance, clarity, form.

Style: oHomophony: Melody with accompaniment (harmony). oBalanced phrases: musical structure with two or more phrases (musical sentences that convey ideas) of equal length and similar tension oSimple harmony: Two or more notes played together pleasingly, e.g. triads oClear cadences: Cadence with clear conclusion (Authentic V-I, Plagal IV-I)

Key Composers: Haydn (father of string quartet and symphony), Mozart (prodigy, famous for his nine symphonies), early Beethoven RomanGc (1820–1900)

20.1 Magnets and Magnetic Fields Magnets and Magnetic poles -Magnet: An object surrounded by a magnetic field and has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt).
◼ A compass needle is simply a bar magnet which is supported at its center of gravity so that it can rotate freely.
Magnetic poles: the area of a magnet where the magnetic effect is stronges -Every magnet is polarized.
Every magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).
N pole is the north -seeking pole, and S pole is the south -seeking pole.
◼ Between m agnets, Like Poles Repel; Unlike Poles Attract.
Magnetic poles always appear in pairs.
Monopoles of magnet do not exist.
Magnetism and Magnetic domain -Ferromagnetism: Iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys, show strong magnetic effects.
Source of ferromagnetism: ◼ The spinning and orbiting motion of the electrons make each atom a tiny magnet.
◼ A cluster of billions of atoms that all have magnetic fields that are lines up in the same way.
So they form a magnetic domain.
Each domain is like a tiny magnet.
◼ Magneti zation:  An unmagnetized piece of iron is made up of domains that are randomly arranged.
 In a magnet, the domains are aligned in one direction (down), and may be altered in size by the magnetization process.
Induced Magnetism: ◼ Both N/S magnetic poles attract metal such as iron, steel.
◼ Unmagnetized materials such as steel and iron acquire two opposite magnetic poles when placed in neighborhood of a magnet.
That is how magnetism is induced.
Making a magnet ◼ Place the unmagnetized material near a magnet.
This gains weak magnetism.
◼ Electromagnet: Make direct current passing through a coil of wire placed outside the materials.
Hard and Soft magnetic materials: Depending on how well they keep their magnetism ◼ Hard magnetic materials  Difficult to magnetized but do not readily lose their magnetism.
 Used for permanent magnets Examples: Steel, and alloys called Alnico, Alcomax and Magnadur ◼ Soft magnetic materials  Relatively easy t magnetize, but their magnetism is only temporary.
 Used for temporary magnets.
They are used in the cores of electromagnets and transformers, because their magnetic effect can be “switched ” on or off or reversed easily.
Examples: Iron(soft iron) and Mumetal -Non -magnetic materials: Include metals such as brass, copper, zinc, tin, and aluminum, as well as non -metals.
Demagnetize a magnet  Drop a magnet on the floor or strike it with a hammer.
The principle is to jar the domains into randomness and the magnet loses some or all of its magnetism.
 Heating a permanent magnet.
The principle is that raising the temperature increases the random thermal motion of atoms, which tends to randomize the domains.
Above a certain temperature, it loses the property of ferromagnetism.
Magnetic field lines-Magnetic Field: the region around a magnet where the magnetic force is exerted.
Experiment s:  Magnetic Field can be investigated using a small compass.
The direction of the magnetic field B at any point is the same as the direction indicated by this compass.
 Magnetic Field can be mapped out by iron filings.
The iron fillings line u p.
Field B is strong where lines are dense and weak where lines are sparse.
Magnetic field lines (They are three -dimensional ): Imaginary lines to map out the magnetic field around a magnet.
The field direction, is defined as the direction in which the force on a N pole would act.

Left: a bar magnet Right: a horse shoe magnet ◼ Direction of arrows  Outside the magnet: from N to S  Inside the magnet: from S to N  A compass placed at any point: tangent to the line of force passing through that point ◼ Density of lines represent s how strong the magnetic field is.
Around two magnets (Combined field) - Close to other materials ◼ Glass: no reaction ◼ Ferromagnetic material:  The field lines become concentrated within the material.
 The end closest to the N pole of magnet become s the S pole of the material.
Magnetic field lines ( in 3D vision ):Uniform magnetic field.
Magnetic field between two wide poles of a magnet is nearly uniform, except near the edges.
Earth as a magnet-Earth ’s magnetism is due to the circulation of the molten metal within Earth ’s core ◼ The earth is a large weak magnet with the magnetic S -seeking pole under a point in Canada.
Magnetic Declination: The angular difference between the direction of a compass needle (which points along the magnetic field lines) at any location and true (geographical) north.
The angle of dip or The angle of inclination: The angle that the Earth’s magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point.
The Earth’s magnetic field at most locations is not tangent to the Earth’s surface.
Magnetic poles reverse themselves periodically.
Earth’s north magnetic pole has been moving over time, on the order of 10 km per year in recent decades.
Magnetism in rocks solidified at various times in the past (age determined by radioactive dating) suggested that poles reversed direction 400 times over the last 330 million years.
20.2 Electric currents produce magnetic fields Magnetic field around a wire-Oersted’s Experiment: Oersted (1777 -1851) discover ed in 1820.
This experiment suggests that m agnetism and electricity are related.
⚫ The compass needle deflects if (and only if) the wire carries an electric current ⚫ Whenever he turned on the electricity, the compass needles lined up in a circle around the wire.
⚫ Iron filings also align along the direction of the magnetic field lines near a straight current carrying wire.
Magnetic field around a wire: If an electric current is passed through a wire, a weak magnetic field is produced.
The magnetic field has these features: ◼ the magnetic field lines are circles ◼ the field is strongest close to the wire ◼ increasing the current increases the strength of the field.
Direction of the current (I) determines the direction of the magnetic field (B).

title: Chapter 7 — – Two Kinds of Mass & Einstein’s Theory of Gravity
points: 1. Two Types of Mass A. Inertial Mass
What is it?
Inertial mass measures how much an object resists a change in motion when a force is applied.
Think of it as how “stubborn” an object is when you try to push it.
How to measure it?
You apply a force to the object and measure how much it accelerates.
If you push two objects with the same force, the heavier one (larger inertial mass) will accelerate less.
B. Gravitational Mass What is it?
Gravitational mass tells us how strongly an object interacts with the force of gravity.
Use a balance scale (like when you weigh something on Earth).
Formula (from Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation):
C. Are These Two Masses the Same?
Yes! According to the Principle of Equivalence, inertial mass = gravitational mass.
Einstein used this idea as the foundation for his theory of gravity.
2. Einstein’s Theory of Gravity
A. Gravity is Not a Force (in Einstein’s view)
Einstein said gravity isn’t a pulling force like Newton thought.
Instead, mass bends space, and objects move along this curved space.

title: Force and Motion Introduction to Force
points: Definition: A force is a push or pull on an object that can change the object’s velocity or cause deformation.

Types of Interaction:
System: The object receiving the force.

Field Forces: Act over a distance without physical contact (e.g., gravity).
(Gravity): The force of attraction between Earth and an object.
Direction: Toward Earth’s center.
Magnitude: (g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth).
​ (Normal Force): The perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface.
Direction: Perpendicular to the surface.
​ (Spring Force): The force exerted by a compressed or stretched spring.
Direction: Opposite the displacement.
(Tension Force): The pull exerted by a taut string, rope, or cable.
Direction: Along the string, away from the object.
​ (Friction Force): The force opposing motion between surfaces in contact.
Direction: Parallel to the surface and opposite to motion.
Thrust: A general force moving objects (e.g., rockets, planes).
Direction: Same as the object’s acceleration.
Gravity and Weight Gravity: A field force that depends on the gravitational pull between two masses.
Weight (W): The gravitational force acting on an object’s mass.
Direction: Downward (toward Earth).

Same Direction: Add magnitudes.
Opposite Direction: Subtract magnitudes.

Newton’s Laws of Motion Newton’s First Law (Law of Inertia):
An object remains at rest or in constant motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
Inertia: The resistance of an object to change in its motion; directly proportional to mass.
Newton’s Second Law (Law of Acceleration):
The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
Units: kg (mass), N (force), m/s² (acceleration).
Newton’s Third Law (Law of Action- Reaction pairs):
If object A exerts force on object B, then object B exerts an equal but opposite force on force A

title: Friction What is Friction?
points: Friction Force: A force that opposes the motion or the tendency of motion between two surfaces.
Caused by: Irregularities in the surfaces in contact.
Direction: Always parallel to the surface and opposite to the direction of motion or the tendency of motion.
Factors Affecting Friction
Nature of Surfaces:
Smooth vs. Rough Surfaces:
Rough surfaces create more friction because they interlock more.
Smooth surfaces create less friction.
The greater the normal force (the force pushing the surfaces together), the greater the friction.
Friction increases when surfaces are rougher and when more force is applied to press the surfaces together.
Static vs. Kinetic Friction
Acts when two surfaces are not moving relative to each other, but there is a tendency for motion.
Maximum static friction (): The maximum force before an object begins to move.

title: Addition of Vectors----Graphical Methods
points: A. Tip-to-Tail Method The resultant/net is the sum of two or more vectors
Commutative: A ⃑ +B ⃑ =B ⃑ +A ⃑
To find the resultant:
1. Move the tail of one vector to the head of another vector without changing the magnitude or direction of the vector
2. The resultant points from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second (last)vector.
Vectors are in one straight line
The magnitude of the vector sum is not always greater than the magnitude of either contributing vector.
The magnitude of resultant of two vectors is never greater than the sum of magnitude of two individual vectors.
Resultant of more than one vector
If three or more vectors form a closed polygon, there is no resultant.
B. Parallelogram Method Place component vectors tail-to-tail
Use the two vectors as adjacent sides and construct a parallelogram
The diagonal from the common origin is the resultant vector
